1Read the sequences & the level

T2 = water bright (CSF, oedema, healthy disc all white); T1 = anatomy, fat bright, CSF dark. A healthy disc is bright on T2; a degenerate/desiccated disc goes dark ("black disc"). Count levels from the sacrum or the last rib. Identify the conus (~L1) — below it the sciatica generators are disc, lateral recess and foramen.

T2 sagittal: disc hydration, canal calibre, thecal sac shape
T2 axial: paracentral vs foraminal disc, root compression
T1: marrow, fat planes, subtle foraminal narrowing
2Disc herniation nomenclature

A spectrum of disc displacement beyond the vertebral margins:

◐Bulge
Symmetrical extension >25% of the disc circumference; broad-based, not focal — usually degenerative and often asymptomatic.
▶Protrusion
Focal (<25%); the base against the parent disc is wider than the herniated dome. Contained by outer annulus.
◤Extrusion
Neck narrower than the herniated material (mushroom shape); through the annulus. A free fragment that separates = sequestration.
3Which root? Traversing vs exiting

The exiting root leaves under its own-numbered pedicle high in the foramen; the traversing root heads down to exit at the level below and sits medially in the lateral recess.

Paracentral (posterolateral) disc — commonest→hits the TRAVERSING root (e.g. L4/5 disc → L5 root)
Far-lateral / foraminal disc→hits the EXITING root (e.g. L4/5 disc → L4 root)

Dermatomes to correlate: L5 — dorsum of foot & big toe, weak dorsiflexion/EHL, no reflex change. S1 — sole & lateral foot, weak plantarflexion, reduced ankle jerk. Always match the images to the clinical level: findings are common in the asymptomatic.

📷 Image placeholder — Axial T2 at L4/5 showing a left paracentral disc protrusion effacing the lateral recess and compressing the traversing L5 root; contrast with a foraminal disc catching the exiting root.
4Stenosis & neurogenic claudication

Central canal, lateral recess or foraminal narrowing (disc + facet hypertrophy + ligamentum flavum buckling) crowds the roots. On axial T2 the thecal sac loses its normal ovoid shape and CSF is effaced.

Bilateral leg pain on walking/standing, eased by flexion or sitting; "shopping-trolley sign" (leans on trolley)→Neurogenic claudication from central stenosis

Distinguish from vascular claudication: vascular pain is relieved by simply stopping (not posture), pulses are absent, and it is unaffected by spinal flexion. Neurogenic pain needs flexion (walking uphill/cycling is tolerated, downhill worse).

🚩 Cauda equina syndrome is the emergency you must never miss: bilateral sciatica, saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention with overflow incontinence, faecal incontinence and reduced anal tone/sensation. It demands emergency (same-day) MRI whole lumbosacral spine and urgent surgical decompression — delay causes permanent bladder/bowel and sexual dysfunction. Do not wait for outpatient imaging.
5MRI safety & when to image

MRI uses a strong static magnetic field — screen for pacemakers/ICDs, cochlear implants, ferromagnetic aneurysm clips, metallic ocular foreign bodies and check implant MR-conditional status. No ionising radiation, so preferred in young patients. It is contrast-free for disc disease (gadolinium reserved for post-op scar vs recurrent disc, infection or tumour); gadolinium is cautioned in severe renal impairment.

When NOT to image: uncomplicated acute sciatica <6 weeks without red flags — manage conservatively. Image if red flags, progressive/severe neurology, or surgery/injection is being planned. Report findings against symptoms, because bulges and degeneration are ubiquitous in pain-free people.

🎓 Below L1/L2 there is no cord to compress — only roots and the cauda equina. A single disc can produce different syndromes depending on where it herniates: paracentral catches the traversing root, foraminal catches the exiting root, and a large central extrusion can crush the whole cauda equina. Let the clinical dermatome pick the culprit, not the prettiest disc on the scan.

Metastatic spinal cord compression (MSCC) is an oncological emergency. In any patient with cancer (or an unknown primary) who develops new back pain with evolving neurology, an MRI of the WHOLE spine is the urgent, gold-standard investigation — it must be obtained within 24 hours because the neurological function present at the time of treatment is the single best predictor of the final outcome.

1Why whole spine, and why urgent

MSCC arises when a vertebral body metastasis extends posteriorly into the epidural space and compresses the thecal sac and cord. The primaries to remember are breast, lung, prostate, myeloma and renal. The thoracic spine is the commonest site, but deposits are frequently at multiple levels — a second, clinically silent compression higher up will be missed on a targeted scan, which is exactly why the entire spine is imaged and why radiotherapy/surgical planning depends on it.

Cancer patient + new or worsening back pain + any new neurology→treat as MSCC until an MRI whole spine excludes it
2The clinical sequence

Symptoms evolve in a recognisable order, and recognising the early ones is what saves cord function:

Back pain — usually the earliest symptom; classically progressive, worse on lying flat, at night, or on coughing/straining (raised epidural venous pressure).
Limb weakness — a later, more ominous sign; symmetrical or asymmetrical, with upgoing plantars if compression is above the conus.
Sensory level — a demonstrable dermatomal level of altered sensation localises the lesion.
Bladder & bowel dysfunction — a late feature (retention with overflow, constipation, painless incontinence); once present, prognosis for recovery is poor.

3Reading the MRI

Four findings confirm MSCC:

🦴Marrow replacement
Metastases replace normal fatty marrow — low signal on T1 against the bright background of surrounding fat.
🎯Epidural mass
Soft-tissue tumour in the epidural space indenting the thecal sac and effacing CSF around the cord.
↔️Cord displacement
The cord is pushed away from the mass and may be flattened or deformed at the level of compression.
⚡Cord signal change
High T2 signal within the compressed cord indicates oedema/myelopathy — a marker of established injury.
4Immediate management
Suspected MSCC→MRI whole spine within 24 h + start treatment in parallel, do not wait
Dexamethasone — high-dose oral/IV steroid started immediately to reduce peri-tumoural oedema; always co-prescribe a PPI for gastric protection (and monitor glucose).
Lie flat with spinal precautions — nurse flat / log-roll until spinal stability is known, to protect the cord.
Refer to the MSCC coordinator — urgent oncology/spinal referral to decide between surgical decompression (mechanically unstable spine, single-level disease, good performance status) and radiotherapy.
Supportive care — analgesia, VTE prophylaxis, bladder management (catheter for retention), pressure-area care.

Why the clock matters: outcome tracks the neurology present at treatment. A patient still walking has a good chance of staying mobile; once paraplegic, function rarely recovers. Speed is therapeutic.

📷 Image placeholder — Axial T2 MRI at the level of compression: epidural tumour encircling and flattening the cord with loss of the surrounding bright CSF ring, contrasted with a normal axial section showing a rounded cord surrounded by CSF.
5MRI safety before the scan

MSCC imaging is urgent but MRI safety screening is never skipped. Check for absolute/relative contraindications: older or non-conditional cardiac pacemakers/ICDs, cochlear implants, certain intracranial aneurysm clips, and metallic intra-ocular foreign bodies (ask about metalwork/grinding). Warn about the enclosed bore and noise in claustrophobic patients. If MRI is genuinely contraindicated or unavailable, CT (with myelography if needed) is the fallback.

🚩 Red flag: ANY patient with known or suspected cancer who reports new or progressively worsening back pain — especially thoracic, nocturnal, or band-like — with or without limb weakness, a sensory level, or bladder/bowel change, has MSCC until an urgent whole-spine MRI proves otherwise. Do not wait for weakness to appear before scanning.
🎓 Pearl: Back pain is the ticket in — it precedes weakness by weeks. The window to preserve walking is while the patient can still walk, so image the whole spine within 24 hours, give dexamethasone straight away, and phone the MSCC coordinator the same day. Treating an ambulant patient keeps them ambulant; treating a paraplegic one usually does not reverse it.

Cauda equina syndrome (CES) is a surgical emergency: compression of the lumbosacral nerve roots below the conus medullaris (~L1/L2) produces a lower motor neurone, areflexic pattern. An urgent MRI of the lumbosacral spine is the definitive investigation — it confirms the compressive lesion, localises the level, and must not be delayed while retention develops.

1Why the cauda equina compresses like this
Below the conus (~L1/L2) the spinal cord has ended; the canal is filled by the free-floating lumbosacral roots (the cauda equina), bathed in CSF within the thecal sac. Because these are nerve roots, not cord, compression produces a peripheral, LMN, areflexic picture — flaccid weakness, reduced reflexes, saddle sensory loss and sphincter failure — rather than the UMN signs of a lesion above the conus.
Central lesion fills the canal→bilateral roots squeezed against the thecal sac
2Red-flag symptoms that mandate the scan
Suspect CES and image immediately if any of these appear — the earlier signs are subtle and easily missed.
Bilateral sciatica or new bilateral leg pain/weakness
Saddle (perineal) anaesthesia — numbness of buttocks, perineum, inner thighs
Bladder dysfunction — early: loss of desire to void / altered sensation of urinary flow; late: painless retention with overflow incontinence
Bowel — incontinence, loss of anal tone/sensation
Sexual dysfunction — loss of genital sensation, erectile/ejaculatory failure

3Causes — one dominates
The commonest cause is a large central disc herniation at L4/5 or L5/S1. The MRI is chosen to identify the lesion and exclude the sinister differentials.
💽Central disc
Large central prolapse L4/5 or L5/S1 — the classic culprit
🎗️Tumour
Metastatic or primary spinal/root tumour filling the canal
🦠Abscess / haematoma
Epidural abscess (fever, IVDU, immunosuppressed) or post-procedure haematoma
🩹Trauma / stenosis
Burst fracture, retropulsed fragment, or severe degenerative canal stenosis
4CES-incomplete vs CES-retention
Grading guides urgency and prognosis. CES-I (incomplete): altered urinary sensation, difficulty initiating/poor stream, but voluntary control preserved — decompress promptly, outcomes better. CES-R (retention): painless urinary retention with overflow incontinence and insensate bladder — worse prognosis. The whole point of early imaging is to catch the patient at the CES-I stage, before they progress to established retention.
Altered sensation, still voiding→CES-I — scan now, don't wait for retention
5Bedside work-up alongside the scan
While arranging MRI, do a PR examination (anal tone, squeeze, perianal sensation) and a post-void bladder scan (a high residual supports retention). Document a full neurological exam of the lower limbs and perineum — the baseline matters medicolegally and for tracking progression. These do not replace or delay imaging.
6Management — decompress fast
Suspected CES = emergency MRI (whole spine or lumbosacral) obtained out of hours if necessary, plus immediate referral to spinal surgery. Definitive treatment is urgent surgical decompression — ideally within 48 hours of onset, and sooner for incomplete CES to preserve function. Delay risks permanent bladder, bowel and sexual dysfunction.
MRI confirms compressive lesion→emergency decompression, ideally <48h

7MRI safety before scanning
MRI uses a powerful static magnetic field — screen every patient: cardiac pacemakers/ICDs, cochlear implants, intracranial aneurysm clips, metallic foreign bodies (especially intra-orbital), and certain neurostimulators may contraindicate the scan. Ask about recent surgery and implants, remove ferromagnetic objects, and check pregnancy status. Gadolinium contrast (used if tumour/abscess suspected) is relatively contraindicated in severe renal impairment.
🚩 Never wait for established painless retention to "confirm" CES — that is the point at which the prognosis worsens. Any red-flag symptom (bilateral sciatica, saddle anaesthesia, altered urinary sensation, bowel/sexual dysfunction) warrants immediate MRI and a same-hour spinal surgery referral, day or night.
🎓 Time is nerve root: the scan you do at the CES-incomplete stage saves bladder, bowel and sexual function. If you find yourself waiting until morning or waiting for the patient to go into retention, you have already lost the window.
Spinal infection is a diagnosis you must not miss: untreated discitis / spondylodiscitis can progress to an epidural abscess with cord compression and permanent neurological injury. MRI with gadolinium is the gold-standard investigation — it detects the infection earlier than plain films or CT, defines the extent, and reveals any collection compressing the cord or thecal sac.
1Pathophysiology — how bugs reach the spine
Most pyogenic spinal infection is haematogenous: bacteria seed the vascular vertebral endplate, then spread into the avascular disc and the adjacent vertebral body. Staphylococcus aureus is the commonest organism. Key risk factors are IV drug use, diabetes, immunosuppression, bacteraemia (e.g. endocarditis, indwelling lines) and recent spinal instrumentation/surgery. Because the disc has no direct blood supply in adults, infection classically bridges two vertebrae across the disc space — the anatomical fact that underlies the key exam discriminator below.
Endplate seeding → disc → opposite endplate→two adjacent vertebrae + the disc between them light up = pyogenic discitis
2MRI findings — what to describe
Look for: T2 hyperintensity of the disc with loss of the normal internal cleft; vertebral endplate marrow oedema that is low on T1, high on T2/STIR in the two vertebrae flanking the disc; loss/erosion of endplate definition; and, after gadolinium, enhancement of the disc, vertebral bodies and paravertebral soft tissues. The most dangerous finding is an epidural abscess — a rim-enhancing collection in the epidural space compressing the cord or thecal sac. Always comment on cord signal (myelomalacia/oedema) and the degree of canal compromise.
T1 low marrow signal in adjacent vertebraeT2/STIR high disc + endplate oedemaPost-Gad disc/vertebral + rim-enhancing epidural collection

3The discriminators — infection vs tumour vs TB
The single most useful rule: infection CROSSES the disc space (endplate-to-endplate involvement of two vertebrae and the disc between them), whereas metastatic/malignant disease tends to SPARE the disc and involve the vertebral body and posterior elements while leaving the disc height and signal preserved. TB (Pott’s disease) is a distinct pattern: it predominantly destroys the vertebral bodies with relative disc sparing, involves multiple levels including subligamentous spread, forms large paraspinal / psoas “cold” abscesses, and produces anterior wedge collapse with an angular kyphosis (gibbus deformity).
🦠Pyogenic discitis
Crosses the disc; endplate oedema in 2 vertebrae + high-signal disc; S. aureus commonest.
🫁TB / Pott’s
Vertebral bodies with disc sparing, psoas cold abscess, gibbus deformity.
🎯Malignancy
Spares the disc; involves body + pedicles/posterior elements; multiple non-contiguous levels.
⚠️Epidural abscess
Rim-enhancing epidural collection compressing cord/thecal sac — surgical emergency.
4Management — get the organism, treat long, decompress if needed
Send blood cultures (positive in a large proportion and may spare the patient a biopsy) and inflammatory markers (raised CRP/ESR). If cultures are negative, arrange image-guided (CT-guided) biopsy of the disc/endplate for microbiology before or alongside antibiotics wherever safe — targeted therapy needs the organism. Treatment is a prolonged course of antibiotics (typically weeks, often ~6 weeks or longer, guided by sensitivities), initially IV. Surgery (decompression/drainage ± stabilisation) is reserved for epidural abscess with neurology, cord compression, progressive deformity/instability, or failure of medical therapy. Remember MRI safety: screen for pacemakers, ferromagnetic implants, cochlear implants and metallic foreign bodies, and check renal function before gadolinium.
🚩
The triad of back pain + fever + neurology (limb weakness, sensory level, bladder/bowel dysfunction) suggests an epidural abscess with cord compression. This — and spinal infection with sepsis — is a surgical emergency: urgent MRI whole spine, blood cultures, IV antibiotics, and emergency decompression/drainage. Do not wait for markers or a biopsy to escalate.
🎓 Exam pearl. If a lesion crosses the disc space and lights up both adjacent endplates, call infection; if it spares the disc and hits the pedicles, think malignancy; if it destroys vertebral bodies with a psoas cold abscess and gibbus, think TB.
MRI__Musculoskeletal — Joints:
MRI is the best test for internal derangement of the knee — the menisci, cruciate and collateral ligaments, and articular cartilage. None of these soft tissues are seen on X-ray, which shows only bone (and indirect signs like an effusion or a Segond avulsion). On MRI, normal menisci and ligaments are uniformly low signal (dark) on all sequences; tears announce themselves as abnormal high (bright) signal or loss of the normal dark structure. Read fluid-sensitive fat-saturated sequences (PD/T2 FS) for oedema, bruising and tears.

1Meniscal tear

The normal meniscus is a low-signal (dark) triangle. A tear is abnormal linear high signal within the meniscus that reaches the articular surface (grade 3 signal). Signal that does not touch a surface is degeneration, not a tear.

Twisting injury with a planted foot, then locking + effusion→suspect meniscal tear; MRI to confirm and localise
Bright line reaching the superior or inferior articular surface = tear.
Bucket-handle tear: a longitudinal fragment displaces into the intercondylar notch, lying under the PCL — the "double PCL sign" on sagittal images.
A truncated/absent meniscal body with a fragment in the notch ("absent bow-tie") also signals a displaced bucket-handle tear.
2ACL tear

The anterior cruciate ligament normally runs as taut, straight, dark fibres from the posterolateral femur to the anterior tibia. A tear shows discontinuous, wavy or absent fibres with surrounding high signal/oedema.

Pivot/deceleration injury, an audible "pop", rapid tense haemarthrosis, positive Lachman→ACL rupture until proven otherwise
Bone bruising (marrow oedema) at the lateral femoral condyle and posterolateral tibial plateau — the "kissing" pattern from the pivot mechanism.
Anterior tibial translation — the tibia slides forward relative to the femur.
Segond fracture — a small avulsion off the lateral tibial rim, highly associated with ACL rupture (visible on X-ray too).

3The other ligaments & the unhappy triad
🩹PCL tear
Thick dark ligament becomes thickened/high-signal; dashboard injury or hyperextension; posterior sag/drawer.
🦵MCL injury
Oedema/high signal along the medial collateral from a valgus force; tender over the medial joint line.
↔️LCL injury
Lateral collateral high signal from a varus force; part of posterolateral corner injuries.
😣Unhappy triad
Valgus + rotation injury: ACL + MCL + medial meniscus torn together — the classic examined combination.

Also look for cartilage defects (fissuring/thinning of the bright articular cartilage) and osteochondral injury (a bone-plus-cartilage fragment with underlying marrow oedema).

🚩 A truly locked knee that cannot fully extend suggests a displaced bucket-handle meniscal tear mechanically blocking the joint and needs urgent orthopaedic referral. A knee dislocation is a limb-threatening emergency — the popliteal artery can be injured; check pulses, ankle-brachial index and arrange CT/MR angiography even if pulses seem present.
4When to image & MRI safety

Acute knee injuries are assessed clinically first, using the Ottawa knee rules to decide who needs an X-ray for fracture (age ≥55, isolated patellar tenderness, fibular head tenderness, inability to flex to 90°, or inability to weight-bear four steps). MRI is for suspected soft-tissue injury or surgical planning, not the first-line acute test. Remember MRI safety: it uses a strong magnet, so screen for pacemakers/ICDs, cochlear implants, ferromagnetic aneurysm clips and metallic foreign bodies; there is no ionising radiation.

🎓 Menisci and ligaments are meant to be uniformly dark on MRI — anything bright is your abnormality. "Signal reaching the surface" makes a meniscal tear; "wavy/absent fibres with a lateral-condyle bone bruise" makes an ACL tear; and a fragment sitting under the PCL ("double PCL sign") is a displaced bucket-handle tear until proven otherwise.

Most shoulder pain is managed conservatively; MRI is reserved for when the diagnosis is unclear, symptoms are refractory, or surgery is being considered. MRI (with MR arthrography when labral pathology is suspected) is the workhorse for the two great soft-tissue territories of the shoulder: the rotator cuff and the glenoid labrum. This subtab walks the interpretive pathway from tendon to labrum, then the traps that catch students.

1Know the four cuff tendons and who tears first

The rotator cuff is a musculotendinous cuff of four muscles that dynamically centre the humeral head in the glenoid: Supraspinatus (abduction initiation, superior), Infraspinatus (external rotation, posterior), Teres minor (external rotation, posteroinferior) and Subscapularis (internal rotation, anterior). Mnemonic SITS.

Supraspinatus is by far the most commonly torn — it runs through the narrow subacromial outlet and is worn by impingement and its watershed ("critical zone") hypovascularity ~1 cm from its footprint on the greater tuberosity.

Best plane for supraspinatus: oblique coronal (fluid-sensitive fat-sat / T2 or PD).
Best plane for subscapularis and biceps: axial.
2Grade the cuff: tendinopathy vs partial vs full-thickness

The whole question is: is there signal, and is there a fluid-signal gap?

Increased intratendinous signal, thickened tendon, NO fluid gap, fibres intact→Tendinopathy (degeneration, not a tear)
Focal fluid signal reaching one surface (bursal or articular) but not through the full thickness→Partial-thickness tear
Fluid-signal gap traversing the ENTIRE tendon, bursa communicating with joint, tendon retraction→Full-thickness tear

Signs of chronic / irreparable tear: tendon retraction to or medial to the glenoid, and muscle atrophy with fatty infiltration (best judged on the sagittal oblique "Y" view, graded by Goutallier). Fatty infiltration does not reverse after repair — it is the key surgical prognostic marker.

3Impingement, bursitis and acromial shape

Subacromial impingement is the mechanical crowding of the supraspinatus under the coraco-acromial arch. Look for subacromial–subdeltoid bursitis (bright fluid in the bursa above the cuff on fluid-sensitive sequences), subacromial spurs, and os acromiale.

Acromial morphology (Bigliani, on sagittal oblique): Type I flat, Type II curved, Type III hooked — the hooked type is associated with impingement and cuff tears.

4The labrum: why MR arthrography

The fibrocartilaginous labrum deepens the shallow glenoid and anchors the capsule, glenohumeral ligaments and long head of biceps. Labral tears are hard to see on plain MRI because torn fibrocartilage abuts fibrocartilage. MR arthrography — dilute intra-articular gadolinium — distends the joint and outlines contrast tracking into a tear, making it the gold standard for labral and partial articular-surface cuff pathology.

⚓Bankart lesion
Tear of the anteroinferior labrum after anterior dislocation. A bony Bankart additionally fractures the anteroinferior glenoid rim.
🔨Hill–Sachs
Impaction fracture of the posterosuperolateral humeral head against the glenoid rim — the mirror injury of a Bankart.
↕️SLAP tear
Superior Labrum Anterior to Posterior, involving the biceps anchor. Typical of overhead athletes / traction injury; contrast undercuts the superior labrum.

5Other MRI diagnoses and MRI safety

Adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder): thickening and oedema of the axillary recess and rotator interval, thickened coracohumeral ligament; clinically global restriction of active AND passive movement, classically in diabetics. Calcific tendinitis: hydroxyapatite in supraspinatus — low signal on all MRI sequences (better seen on plain radiograph/US). Biceps pathology: long-head tendinosis, subluxation/dislocation from the bicipital groove (often with subscapularis tears), or an empty groove in rupture.

MRI safety: screen every patient for ferromagnetic hazards — cardiac pacemakers/ICDs (unless MR-conditional), cochlear implants, ferromagnetic intracranial aneurysm clips, metallic intra-ocular foreign bodies. The magnet is always on. In arthrography, use aseptic technique and confirm no gadolinium contraindication (severe renal impairment — nephrogenic systemic fibrosis).

🚩 An acute massive cuff tear with pseudoparalysis (patient cannot actively abduct or hold the arm elevated despite a full passive range) needs urgent surgical referral. Likewise, an anterior shoulder dislocation with axillary nerve injury (loss of the regimental-badge sensation / deltoid weakness) or any sign of neurovascular compromise is an emergency — image and refer, do not just reassure.
🎓 Two words unlock most shoulder MRIs: gap and gadolinium. A fluid-signal gap across a tendon means a full-thickness cuff tear (retraction + fatty muscle infiltration = chronic/irreparable), while gadolinium arthrography is what you order when you suspect the labrum — Bankart below, SLAP above, always hunting the paired Hill–Sachs.

MRI is the gold-standard problem-solver for the painful hip, chiefly because it images bone marrow. That single strength lets it reveal fractures, infarcts and infiltration that plain films — which only show cortical bone and gross density change — simply cannot see. Its headline role in UK practice is catching the occult hip fracture in the elderly faller with a normal X-ray.

Elderly fall, hip pain, cannot weight-bear, X-ray NORMAL→Do NOT discharge — MRI to exclude occult neck of femur fracture
1Occult hip fracture — the flagship indication

Up to ~10% of femoral neck fractures are invisible on initial radiographs. In an elderly patient with a clinical fracture but a normal X-ray, MRI is the gold standard: it shows a low-signal fracture line surrounded by high-signal marrow oedema on fluid-sensitive (STIR/T2 fat-sat) sequences within hours of injury. If MRI is contraindicated or unavailable, CT is the accepted alternative (better cortical detail, but less sensitive for non-displaced fractures and marrow oedema).

T1: linear low-signal fracture line through the femoral neck
STIR/T2 fat-sat: bright marrow oedema (bone bruise) around the line
Extent of line (partial vs complete) guides fixation vs arthroplasty

2Avascular necrosis (osteonecrosis) of the femoral head

Death of femoral head marrow and trabeculae from interrupted blood supply. Classic risk factors: steroids, alcohol, sickle cell disease, and trauma (e.g. displaced neck of femur fracture disrupting the retinacular vessels). MRI is the most sensitive test and detects AVN before X-ray changes or collapse appear. The hallmark is the "double-line sign" on T2 (an inner bright band of granulation tissue and an outer dark sclerotic rim) with subchondral marrow change in the anterosuperior head. MRI staging (e.g. pre-collapse vs subchondral fracture/collapse) determines whether joint-preserving surgery (core decompression) or joint replacement is appropriate.

Serpiginous subchondral line, anterosuperior femoral head
"Double-line sign" on T2 — highly specific for AVN
Look for the subchondral fracture / crescent sign = collapse imminent
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image: coronal T1/T2 of both hips showing a geographic subchondral lesion in the right femoral head with the double-line sign, head still spherical (pre-collapse).
3The other MRI hip problems — a quick map

Beyond fractures and AVN, MRI characterises a range of hip pathology, often distinguishing self-limiting from surgical disease.

💧Transient osteoporosis
Diffuse marrow oedema of the head/neck, self-limiting; mimics AVN but no double-line sign or subchondral fracture. Typically middle-aged men or 3rd-trimester pregnancy.
🔗Labral tear / FAI
Femoroacetabular impingement (cam = femoral head-neck bump; pincer = acetabular over-coverage). MR arthrography best shows the acetabular labral tear in young active adults with groin pain.
🏃Stress fracture
Femoral neck stress fracture in runners/military recruits — marrow oedema ± a line before radiographic change. Tension-side (superolateral) fractures risk displacement.
🎗️Tumour / metastasis
MRI defines marrow-replacing lesions and soft-tissue masses, and detects metastatic deposits (breast, prostate, lung, kidney, thyroid) — pathological fracture risk.
🚩 An elderly patient who cannot weight-bear after a fall with a "normal" X-ray has an occult neck of femur fracture until proven otherwise — image (MRI, or CT) and treat; do NOT discharge. Separately, a femoral neck stress fracture on the tension (superolateral) side can displace and progress to a full fracture — treat as urgent, offload/refer rather than send back to running.
🎓 Remember MRI's two golden roles at the hip: it sees a fracture line and marrow oedema days before the same fracture shows on X-ray, and it catches AVN in its reversible pre-collapse phase via the double-line sign. Marrow oedema is sensitive but non-specific — the surrounding features (fracture line vs double-line vs diffuse transient change) tell you which diagnosis you're looking at.

MRI is the workhorse for the ankle and foot when radiographs are normal but symptoms persist: it shows tendons, ligaments, cartilage, marrow and soft tissue in exquisite detail. Two exam-critical themes dominate — the acutely injured athletic ankle (Achilles, lateral ligaments, osteochondral talar lesions, stress injuries) and the diabetic foot, where MRI is the key test to separate osteomyelitis from Charcot neuroarthropathy.

📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image.
1Sequences & how to read the ankle

Fluid-sensitive fat-suppressed sequences (T2 FS / STIR / PD FS) make oedema, effusion and marrow pathology light up bright; T1 shows anatomy and marrow fat. A simple rule: fat is bright on T1, so normal marrow is bright on T1 — loss of that bright T1 marrow signal is a red flag for infiltration or infection.

Bright on fluid-sensitive, low on T1→oedema, effusion or marrow pathology
T1: anatomy, marrow fat, fibre discontinuity/gaps.
T2/PD FS & STIR: fluid, oedema, tendinopathy, marrow signal.
Post-contrast T1 FS: enhancement — abscess wall, sinus tract, osteomyelitis.
2Achilles tendon — tendinopathy vs rupture

Tendinopathy: fusiform thickening of the tendon with loss of its normal thin low-signal ribbon and increased intrasubstance signal; fibres remain intact. Full-thickness rupture: complete fibre discontinuity with a fluid-filled gap and retracted, wavy tendon ends — clinically the calf squeeze (Simmonds/Thompson) test is positive (no plantarflexion). Measure the gap and tendon-end retraction, as this guides operative vs conservative management.

Discontinuous fibres + fluid gap + positive Thompson→full-thickness rupture
3Ligaments, tendons & talar dome

Lateral ligament sprains: the ATFL is the most commonly injured, followed by the CFL, after inversion injury — look for thickening, discontinuity or oedema. Tibialis posterior tendon dysfunction (tendon degeneration/tear medial to the malleolus) is the classic cause of adult acquired flatfoot. Osteochondral lesions of the talar dome show a subchondral defect with marrow oedema; fluid signal undermining a fragment on fluid-sensitive sequences indicates instability.

Medial hindfoot pain + flat arch + degenerate tib post tendon→tibialis posterior dysfunction (flatfoot)
4Occult fractures & bone stress injuries

MRI detects fractures invisible on radiographs. Bone stress injuries show ill-defined marrow oedema (bright on STIR) progressing to a low-signal fracture line. High-risk sites to name: the tarsal navicular (sagittal stress fracture, prone to non-union) and metatarsal stress fractures (classically the 2nd/3rd "march" fracture). Correlate with focal tenderness and load history.

5The diabetic foot — osteomyelitis vs Charcot

This is the highest-yield distinction. Osteomyelitis in the diabetic foot spreads by contiguous extension from a skin ulcer, so anatomy is everything: pathology under a pressure point with an overlying ulcer/sinus favours infection. Charcot (neuropathic) arthropathy centres on the midfoot (tarsometatarsal / Lisfranc region) with fragmentation, deformity and the classic rocker-bottom foot — and it can closely mimic infection.

🦴Osteomyelitis
Marrow signal replacement: low T1, high T2/STIR, avid enhancement; adjacent ulcer/sinus tract and cortical erosion; secondary soft-tissue oedema/abscess.
🦶Charcot arthropathy
Midfoot deformity, subluxation, rocker-bottom; oedema centred on joints not a single bone; no ulcer or sinus tract; subchondral cysts, debris.
💧Soft-tissue infection
Cellulitis oedema, and abscess = rim-enhancing fluid collection; sinus tract = enhancing tract linking skin to deep tissue/bone.
Marrow T1 replacement + enhancement + ulcer/sinus tract to bone→osteomyelitis over Charcot

6Forefoot & heel pain; MRI safety

Morton's neuroma: a teardrop mass in an intermetatarsal space (commonly 3rd), low-to-intermediate on T2. Plantar fasciitis: thickened proximal plantar fascia (>4 mm) with perifascial oedema at the calcaneal origin. MRI safety: always screen for cardiac pacemakers/ICDs, cochlear implants, intraocular metallic foreign bodies and certain aneurysm clips; the magnet is always on. Gadolinium is used cautiously in severe renal impairment (risk of nephrogenic systemic fibrosis).

🚩 Diabetic foot osteomyelitis or deep soft-tissue infection is limb-threatening — it needs urgent assessment by the multidisciplinary diabetic foot team. A rapidly spreading, systemically unwell foot with gas or fascial-plane fluid raises necrotising infection, a surgical emergency requiring immediate senior review and debridement, not a wait for imaging.
🎓 Let anatomy break the tie in the diabetic foot: pathology under an ulcer or sinus tract with T1 marrow replacement and enhancement means osteomyelitis, whereas joint-centred midfoot fragmentation with a rocker-bottom deformity and no skin breach points to Charcot — and remember the two can coexist.

MRI is the highest-sensitivity investigation of the wrist, prized in medical-school teaching for one headline indication: the clinically suspected scaphoid fracture with a normal X-ray. It resolves soft-tissue and marrow pathology that plain films and CT cannot, but its most life-changing use is confirming an occult fracture before a hidden scaphoid slips into avascular necrosis or non-union.

1The occult scaphoid fracture — the classic case

A young adult falls on an outstretched hand (FOOSH) and has tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox, pain on axial loading of the thumb, and pain on ulnar deviation. The initial wrist X-ray (including dedicated scaphoid views) is reported as normal. Up to a quarter of true scaphoid fractures are invisible on the first film because the fracture line has not yet displaced or resorbed.

Snuffbox tenderness + normal X-ray→Immobilise and re-image — MRI is the gold standard

MRI is the definitive next step because it is both the most sensitive and most specific test for an occult scaphoid fracture. It detects the fracture at day one, when a fracture line, cortical breach, and surrounding bone-marrow oedema are all visible.

T1: low-signal (dark) fracture line crossing the normally bright fatty marrow of the scaphoid.
T2 / STIR (fat-suppressed): high-signal (bright) marrow oedema highlighting the fracture and surrounding trabecular injury.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image: coronal T1 of the wrist showing a low-signal line through the scaphoid waist against bright marrow, with the corresponding STIR sequence showing bright oedema; label the proximal pole, waist, and distal pole.
2Why the scaphoid is so dangerous — retrograde blood supply

The scaphoid receives its blood retrogradely: the dorsal carpal branch of the radial artery enters distally and perfuses the bone from the waist back towards the proximal pole. A fracture through the waist or proximal pole cuts off the proximal fragment's supply.

Missed / untreated waist fracture→Proximal-pole AVN and non-union

This is why an occult fracture cannot be shrugged off: a missed scaphoid fracture leads to avascular necrosis (AVN) of the proximal pole, non-union, and eventually a scaphoid non-union advanced collapse (SNAC) pattern of wrist arthritis. Early MRI diagnosis lets you cast (or fix) the fracture that needs treatment and discharge the genuinely normal wrist, sparing weeks of unnecessary immobilisation.

3The other things MRI wrist looks for

Beyond the scaphoid, MRI is the workhorse for internal derangement — the soft-tissue and cartilage structures invisible on X-ray.

🩹TFCC tear
Triangular fibrocartilage complex — the classic cause of ulnar-sided wrist pain and clicking, worse on gripping and ulnar deviation.
🔗Scapholunate tear
Ligament rupture causing carpal instability; if untreated leads to scapholunate advanced collapse (SLAC wrist) arthritis.
🌙Kienböck's disease
Avascular necrosis of the lunate; MRI shows early marrow signal change long before X-ray sclerosis or collapse appears.
💧Ganglia & tendons
Confirms dorsal/volar ganglion cysts and tendon pathology such as de Quervain's tenosynovitis of the first extensor compartment.

Carpal tunnel syndrome is largely a clinical and nerve-conduction-study diagnosis; MRI is reserved for atypical cases or to look for a space-occupying cause (ganglion, mass) compressing the median nerve.

4MRI safety — before anyone enters the scanner

MRI uses a powerful static magnetic field and radiofrequency pulses — no ionising radiation, which makes it attractive in young patients. Every patient must be safety-screened for ferromagnetic hazards.

Cardiac pacemaker, cochlear implant, metallic intra-ocular foreign body→Potential contraindication — check MR-conditional status before scanning

Ask specifically about metalworkers (orbital metal fragments), aneurysm clips, and implanted devices. The scanner is loud and enclosed, so warn about noise and claustrophobia. Gadolinium contrast (used for MR arthrography of ligament/TFCC tears) needs caution in significant renal impairment.

🚩 A clinically suspected scaphoid fracture with a normal X-ray is never dismissed as "just a sprain." Immobilise in a below-elbow cast/splint and re-image — MRI is the definitive test. Missing it risks avascular necrosis and non-union of the scaphoid, a classic exam and medicolegal pitfall.
🎓 Snuffbox tenderness after a FOOSH with a normal film means treat as a fracture until MRI proves otherwise. MRI wins because it images bone marrow, ligaments and cartilage in one radiation-free study — spotting the occult scaphoid fracture on day one while also excluding TFCC, scapholunate, and lunate pathology.

The elbow is a hinge with a stabilising ligament complex, three tendon groups and three nerves running close to bone. MRI is the workhorse for soft-tissue elbow pain: it grades tendon overuse, defines whether a tendon rupture is partial or complete (which decides surgery), maps ligament and nerve injury, and detects osteochondral lesions long before radiographs. Bright signal on fluid-sensitive sequences (T2 fat-sat, STIR, PD fat-sat) is your friend — it lights up oedema, tears and effusions.

📷 Image placeholder — Coronal PD fat-sat of the elbow labelling common extensor origin (lateral epicondyle), common flexor origin (medial epicondyle), ulnar collateral ligament, and the cubital tunnel.
1Tendon overuse — the epicondylitides

Lateral epicondylitis ("tennis elbow") is far commoner and affects the common extensor origin, principally ECRB (extensor carpi radialis brevis). Medial epicondylitis ("golfer's elbow") affects the common flexor–pronator origin. Despite the "-itis", the pathology is angiofibroblastic tendinosis (degeneration), not true inflammation.

Lateral elbow pain, worse gripping/wrist extension→think common extensor origin / ECRB tendinosis
Tendinosis: tendon thickening with intermediate (grey) signal — bright on fluid-sensitive sequences.
Tear: fluid-signal cleft or focal fibre discontinuity at the origin; can extend into the underlying LCL.
Chronic: adjacent cortical irregularity / enthesophyte at the epicondyle.
2Ligament — ulnar collateral ligament (UCL)

The UCL (medial collateral ligament), especially its anterior bundle, is the primary restraint to valgus stress. It fails in throwing / overhead athletes (baseball pitchers, javelin) causing valgus instability. MR arthrography is most sensitive: intra-articular contrast leaking under a partially detached distal ligament gives the classic "T sign".

Medial pain in a thrower with valgus laxity→UCL injury — request MR arthrogram
3Distal biceps tendon rupture

The distal biceps inserts on the radial tuberosity; rupture typically follows an eccentric load (lifting) in a middle-aged man, giving a "reverse Popeye" (retracted, distally-drawn belly), a palpable gap, and weak supination and flexion. MRI (often the FABS view: Flexed elbow, ABducted shoulder, Supinated forearm) defines complete vs partial and measures retraction — the key surgical determinant.

Complete: fluid-filled gap, tendon retraction proximally, empty tuberosity footprint.
Partial: tendon attenuation / high signal but fibres still tethered to the tuberosity.
📷 Image placeholder — Sagittal fluid-sensitive image showing a complete distal biceps rupture with a fluid-filled gap and proximal tendon retraction; empty radial tuberosity footprint.
4Nerve, osteochondral lesions & effusion

Ulnar nerve at the cubital tunnel (behind the medial epicondyle) is the second commonest entrapment neuropathy after carpal tunnel — MRI shows a thickened, oedematous (T2-bright) nerve, sometimes subluxation. Osteochondritis dissecans (OCD) of the capitellum occurs in adolescent throwers and gymnasts; MRI grades stability and detects loose bodies (Panner disease is the younger, self-limiting osteochondrosis mimic). An elbow effusion displaces the fat pads — on X-ray a posterior fat-pad sign / raised anterior "sail" sign in an adult implies an occult radial head fracture.

🎾Lateral epicondylitis
Common extensor origin / ECRB thickening & high signal.
⚾UCL injury
Valgus instability in throwers; MR arthrogram "T sign".
💪Distal biceps rupture
Weak supination/flexion; complete vs partial decides surgery.
⚡Cubital tunnel syndrome
Ulnar nerve thickening/oedema behind medial epicondyle.
🚩 Distal biceps rupture needs prompt surgical referral — anatomical repair is best within roughly 2–3 weeks before the tendon retracts and scars; delay risks permanent supination weakness. Treat any suspected neurovascular injury and septic arthritis of the elbow (hot, swollen, systemically unwell joint) as emergencies — aspirate/refer before imaging chases anything else.
🎓 MRI safety: always screen for ferromagnetic implants, pacemakers/ICDs, cochlear implants, aneurysm clips and metallic foreign bodies before scanning; gadolinium is avoided in severe renal impairment (NSF risk) and used cautiously in pregnancy. Remember the elbow rule of thumb — lateral = extensors, medial = flexors — and that bright fluid signal is the common thread linking tendinosis, tears, ligament injury, nerve oedema and effusion.
MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft Tissue:
MRI is uniquely sensitive to bone marrow because it images marrow fat and water directly. Normal adult marrow is fatty and therefore bright on T1. Almost any pathological process — oedema, necrosis, tumour — replaces fat with water or cells, producing the universal signature: low T1, high T2/STIR. This makes MRI the tool of choice for occult fractures, avascular necrosis and marrow infiltration long before X-ray changes appear.
1The marrow signal rule
Adult yellow marrow is fatty, so it is bright on T1 (like subcutaneous fat) and suppressed on fat-saturated sequences. A marrow-replacing or oedematous process pushes out fat and adds water: it becomes dark on T1 and bright on T2/STIR. STIR (fat-suppressed) is the workhorse — it nulls the bright fat so oedema and infiltration light up conspicuously. Learn the pair: low T1 = something has replaced the fat; high STIR = water/oedema present.
Focal low T1 + high STIR + a line→occult fracture with marrow oedema
2Occult fracture & bone stress injury
When clinical suspicion is high but X-ray is normal, MRI shows the fracture line (low signal on all sequences) surrounded by marrow oedema (low T1, high STIR) days before radiographic changes. Classic exam scenarios: the scaphoid after a FOOSH with a normal initial X-ray; the femoral neck/hip in an elderly faller who cannot weight-bear; and sacral insufficiency fractures in osteoporotic or elderly patients presenting as unexplained back/pelvic pain. MRI also grades stress injuries in athletes from marrow oedema alone through to a frank fracture line.
T1 — anatomy & marrow fatSTIR/T2 FS — oedema detectorFracture line — dark on all sequences
📷 Image placeholder — coronal STIR of the hip showing a low-signal fracture line through the femoral neck with surrounding bright marrow oedema, X-ray reported normal.
3Avascular necrosis (osteonecrosis)
Ischaemic death of marrow and trabecular bone — the femoral head is the classic site. MRI detects AVN pre-collapse, before X-ray shows sclerosis or the crescent sign, allowing joint-preserving treatment. The hallmark is the double-line sign on T2: an inner bright rim of hypervascular granulation tissue and an outer dark rim of reactive sclerosis, demarcating the necrotic segment. Remember the risk factors — steroids, alcohol, sickle cell disease, trauma (also SLE, the bends/dysbaric, radiotherapy).
🦴AVN
Subchondral double-line sign; femoral head; steroids/alcohol/sickle cell.
💧Marrow oedema syndrome
Diffuse high STIR, no line; transient osteoporosis of the hip, self-limiting.
🩹Bone bruise
Trabecular microfracture/contusion after trauma; oedema without cortical break.
🎯Infiltration
Marrow replaced by tumour/cells → low T1; mets, myeloma, leukaemia.
4Marrow oedema syndromes & infiltration
Oedema syndromes — transient osteoporosis of the hip and post-traumatic bone bruise/contusion — show marrow oedema without a fracture line and are usually self-limiting. Marrow infiltration/replacement is the sinister group: metastases and myeloma replace bright fatty marrow, appearing dark on T1 (focal deposits or diffuse disease); leukaemia and lymphoma cause diffuse marrow replacement, and physiological red marrow reconversion (anaemia, smokers, athletes) is a mimic that stays brighter than muscle/disc on T1. Whole-body MRI with STIR is now standard for staging myeloma and screening the skeleton for metastatic marrow disease.
📷 Image placeholder — sagittal T1 of the spine showing multiple focal low-signal (darker than intervertebral disc) vertebral deposits replacing the normally bright fatty marrow, consistent with metastatic/myelomatous infiltration.
🚩
Diffuse low-T1 marrow that is darker than adjacent muscle or disc is not physiological — it suggests malignant infiltration (metastases or myeloma) and mandates investigation, with attention to pathological fracture risk. Never forget MRI safety contraindications (non-conditional pacemaker/ICD, certain intracranial clips/metallic foreign bodies, cochlear implants) before requesting the scan.
🎓 Exam pearl. Use marrow as an internal control on T1: normal adult marrow should be brighter than muscle and brighter than the intervertebral disc. If a lesion or diffuse marrow is darker than the disc, think replacement (fracture, tumour, infiltration); the double-line sign means AVN, and a normal X-ray never excludes an occult scaphoid, hip or sacral fracture.

A febrile child with a limp, or a diabetic with a non-healing foot ulcer probing to bone — plain films are normal for the first ~10–14 days, so MRI with gadolinium is the most sensitive and specific test for osteomyelitis and soft-tissue infection. It shows marrow oedema, abscesses and fascial spread long before the cortex breaks down. This subtab teaches you to read the marrow, hunt the abscess, and recognise the one diagnosis you must NOT wait for MRI to make.

1Why MRI, and why X-ray fails early

Bone destruction on plain film needs ~30–50% loss of mineral before it is visible — a ~2-week lag. MRI detects the earliest event, marrow oedema, within days.

Suspected osteomyelitis + normal X-ray→MRI with gadolinium (do not be reassured by the film)
T1: best for anatomy and marrow — normal fatty marrow is bright, infected marrow goes low.
T2 / STIR: fat-suppressed, fluid-sensitive — oedema and pus go bright.
Post-gadolinium T1 fat-sat: viable inflamed tissue enhances; non-enhancing central fluid = abscess/necrosis.
DWI: pus restricts diffusion — helps confirm an abscess.
2Acute osteomyelitis — read the marrow

The core sign is marrow signal replacement: normal bright T1 fat is replaced by confluent low T1, with high T2/STIR and enhancement. Confluent (not just reticular) low-T1 marrow is the most specific pattern.

Periosteal reaction: thin enhancing rim lifted off cortex, often with subperiosteal pus.
Cortical destruction / breach: loss of the normal low-signal cortical line.
Adjacent soft-tissue oedema and sinus tract: enhancing tract to the skin.

Routes tell you where to look:

Haematogenous (children)→Metaphysis of long bones (slow sinusoidal flow); Staph aureus; sickle cell → think Salmonella
Contiguous spread (adults)→Diabetic foot ulcer, pressure sore, penetrating trauma, prosthesis — infection tracks inward from the ulcer
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image: sagittal T1 of the tibia showing confluent low-signal marrow replacing bright fatty marrow in the metaphysis, with adjacent periosteal reaction.
3Chronic osteomyelitis — the named signs

When infection persists, a characteristic architecture develops. Learn these four terms — they are exam gold.

Sequestrum: a fragment of dead, avascular bone — low signal on all sequences, non-enhancing, sitting within pus. Acts as a nidus for relapse.
Involucrum: a shell of new living bone laid down around the sequestrum — it does enhance.
Cloaca: an opening in the involucrum through which pus/sequestrum drains.
Sinus tract: an enhancing channel from bone to skin surface.
Non-enhancing bony fragment in a rim-enhancing cavity→Sequestrum — flag for surgical debridement (antibiotics alone won't sterilise dead bone)
4Soft-tissue infection — a ladder of severity

MRI separates a diffuse skin infection from a drainable collection from a surgical emergency.

🩹Cellulitis
Reticulated (lace-like) subcutaneous oedema — high T2/STIR streaking through fat, diffuse enhancement, NO drainable collection.
💧Abscess
Rim-enhancing fluid collection with a non-enhancing centre and restricted diffusion (bright DWI, dark ADC). Needs drainage.
🔥Pyomyositis
Muscle oedema and enhancement, progressing to intramuscular abscess — often Staph aureus.
🦴Septic arthritis
Joint effusion + synovial enhancement + periarticular marrow oedema. A hot joint is an emergency — aspirate, don't wait for MRI.
⚠️Necrotising fasciitis
Fluid/oedema tracking along DEEP fascia, thick (>3mm) fascial enhancement or non-enhancement (necrosis), and gas. A CLINICAL diagnosis — MRI must not delay theatre.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image: axial post-gadolinium fat-sat T1 of the thigh showing a rim-enhancing collection with a non-enhancing centre (abscess), alongside diffuse reticulated subcutaneous enhancement (cellulitis).
5Diabetic foot — osteomyelitis vs Charcot

Both give marrow oedema in the diabetic foot; the key is distribution and company.

Osteomyelitis: marrow change centred on a pressure point beneath an ulcer/sinus (e.g. metatarsal head, calcaneus), with a soft-tissue ulcer tracking to bone and secondary signs (sinus tract, cortical erosion, adjacent abscess).
Charcot (neuro-arthropathy): centred on joints, especially the midfoot (Lisfranc/tarsometatarsal), with deformity ("rocker-bottom"), subchondral cysts and debris, and no adjacent skin ulcer or sinus.
Marrow oedema + overlying ulcer probing to bone→Osteomyelitis until proven otherwise
6MRI safety — before anyone goes in the bore

MRI uses a powerful static magnet — safety screening is mandatory.

Ferromagnetic hazards: old pacemakers/ICDs, cochlear implants, intra-ocular metal fragments, some aneurysm clips, metallic foreign bodies.
Gadolinium + poor renal function: risk of nephrogenic systemic fibrosis — check eGFR before contrast.
Gadolinium in pregnancy: avoid unless essential (crosses placenta).
🚩 Necrotising fasciitis is a CLINICAL diagnosis and a surgical emergency. Severe pain out of proportion to skin findings, rapidly spreading erythema, systemic toxicity, and crepitus mean immediate surgical debridement plus broad-spectrum antibiotics — do NOT wait for MRI. Likewise a hot, swollen joint needs urgent aspiration for septic arthritis; imaging must never delay these interventions.
🎓 Pearl: Osteomyelitis lives in the marrow — so let T1 do the talking. Confluent low-T1 marrow that replaces the bright fatty signal is the single most useful MRI sign; oedema on STIR is sensitive but non-specific, while confluent T1 replacement is what makes the diagnosis. In chronic disease, hunt the non-enhancing sequestrum — dead bone antibiotics can't reach, and the reason the surgeon, not the microbiologist, ultimately cures it.

A patient presents with a soft-tissue lump. The single most important question is: could this be a sarcoma? MRI is the imaging workhorse here — not to make the diagnosis (it usually cannot separate benign from malignant on signal alone), but to characterise the mass and locally stage it for the sarcoma MDT. Get the pathway right and outcomes are good; get an unplanned excision ("whoops procedure") and you compromise the patient.

1Spot the red-flag lump — the 2-week-wait sarcoma criteria

Most soft-tissue lumps are benign (lipomas, cysts, ganglia). Urgent referral to a specialist sarcoma unit + urgent MRI is warranted when a lump shows any of the classic red flags. Remember them as size, depth, growth, pain, recurrence.

Lump >5 cm, deep to fascia, rapidly growing, painful, or recurrent→treat as sarcoma until proven otherwise — refer, image, biopsy
🚩 An enlarging deep lump >5 cm is a sarcoma until proven otherwise. Do NOT arrange a local excision "to see what it is".
2Why MRI is the modality of choice

MRI gives superb soft-tissue contrast, so it defines what surgeons and the MDT actually need: the size of the mass, which compartment it sits in, and its relationship to the neurovascular bundle and bone. This is the information that drives surgical planning and limb-sparing resection.

Multiplanar imaging maps the exact anatomical extent and compartment.
Fat-suppressed T2 / STIR highlights oedema and tumour margins.
Post-contrast (gadolinium) shows enhancement, necrosis and vascularity.
Defines relationship to the neurovascular bundle for resectability.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image: axial T1 of the thigh showing a large deep intramuscular soft-tissue mass, annotated with compartment boundaries and its relationship to the femur and femoral neurovascular bundle.
3Characteristic MRI signatures — and the limits of signal

A few lesions have near-diagnostic appearances, but many overlap. Crucially, MRI signal alone cannot reliably separate benign from malignant — which is why tissue is still needed.

🟡Lipoma
Follows subcutaneous fat on ALL sequences (bright T1, suppresses on fat-sat). Thick septa/nodularity raises concern for atypical lipomatous tumour.
🩸Haemangioma
Serpiginous vessels, high T2 signal, often with phleboliths and interspersed fat.
💧Myxoid tumour
Very high T2 signal mimicking a cyst, but shows internal enhancement — a solid mass, not fluid.
⚫PVNS / GCT tendon sheath
Haemosiderin causes low signal and "blooming" artefact on gradient-echo (GRE) sequences.
⚠️Features favouring malignancy
Large size, marked heterogeneity, necrosis, irregular margins and avid but patchy enhancement.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image: gradient-echo sequence of a digit showing low-signal "blooming" of a giant cell tumour of the tendon sheath from haemosiderin deposition.
4Biopsy and staging — the MDT pathway

Because MRI cannot confirm malignancy, image-guided core biopsy is essential. The key surgical principle: the biopsy is planned by the sarcoma MDT and placed along the line of the future resection, so the whole biopsy tract can be excised en bloc. A poorly placed biopsy or an unplanned excision seeds tumour and forces wider, more morbid surgery.

Unknown soft-tissue mass→MRI + planned image-guided core biopsy FIRST — never excise blind
Local staging: MRI of the primary site (size, compartment, margins).
Distant staging: CT chest — sarcomas metastasise haematogenously to lung.
5MRI safety essentials

Before any MRI, screen for the strong magnetic field. Ferromagnetic hazards and certain implants can be dangerous.

Screen for cardiac pacemakers/ICDs, cochlear implants, and metallic foreign bodies (e.g. intra-ocular metal in metalworkers).
Remove all ferromagnetic objects — the projectile effect can be fatal.
Gadolinium contrast: caution in severe renal impairment (nephrogenic systemic fibrosis risk).
🎓 MRI's job in a soft-tissue mass is to characterise and locally stage, not to prove malignancy. The unforgivable error is the "whoops" resection — cutting out a deep >5 cm lump without prior MRI and MDT-planned biopsy. Always: red-flag lump → refer to sarcoma unit → MRI + CT chest → planned core biopsy → definitive surgery.
