Cardiac MRI (CMR) is the gold standard for ventricular volumes, mass and ejection fraction. Because it is so reproducible, it wins whenever an accurate, repeatable number matters over time — tracking chemotherapy cardiotoxicity, deciding on an ICD, or following congenital heart disease. It sees what echo cannot: the right ventricle, poor echo windows, and flow without geometric guesswork.

1Acquire ECG-gated cine images

The heart is imaged with ECG-gated cine SSFP (steady-state free precession) sequences — bright-blood "movie" loops of the beating heart. Acquisition is split across the cardiac cycle using the ECG R-wave as a trigger, and each slice is captured during a breath-hold to remove respiratory motion.

Bright-blood cine (SSFP) → sharp blood–myocardium border for tracing contours
2Use the standard planes

A short-axis stack of contiguous slices from base to apex is the workhorse for volumetry; 2-, 3- and 4-chamber long-axis views assess chambers, valves and wall motion.

Short-axis stack — volumes & mass
4-chamber — all four chambers, AV valves
2-chamber — LV anterior/inferior walls
3-chamber (LVOT) — aortic valve & outflow
📷 Image placeholder — describe the cardiac MRI image: a short-axis mid-ventricular SSFP cine still showing the bright LV blood pool ringed by grey myocardium, with the crescent-shaped RV, at end-diastole.
3Measure volumes by Simpson's method

Endocardial (and epicardial) contours are traced on each short-axis slice at end-diastole and end-systole. Slice areas are multiplied by slice thickness and summed (Simpson's method of discs) — so volumes come from real anatomy with no geometric assumptions, unlike echo which assumes an idealised ellipsoid.

Sum contiguous slices → EDV, ESV, SV, EF and myocardial mass for LV and RV

EF = (EDV − ESV) / EDV. Because contours are traced directly, CMR is far more reproducible than echo for serial monitoring.

4Assess function, valves and flow

Cines show regional wall motion (hypokinesis/akinesis in ischaemia). Phase-contrast sequences quantify velocity and flow — regurgitant volumes/fractions, and the pulmonary-to-systemic flow ratio Qp:Qs for shunts. CMR is superior to echo for the right ventricle and for patients with poor acoustic windows.

📈Serial EF monitoring
Chemo cardiotoxicity — reproducibility catches small true drops
🫀Right ventricle
Complex RV geometry echo struggles with — CMR is the reference
🔧Pre-device / ICD
Accurate EF drives primary-prevention ICD decisions
👶Congenital / shunts
Qp:Qs and RV volumes guide timing of intervention
📷 Image placeholder — describe the cardiac MRI image: a base-to-apex short-axis stack montage with endocardial and epicardial contours traced on each slice, illustrating Simpson's summation of discs for LV volume and mass.

Strengths vs limitations. CMR uses no ionising radiation and needs no geometric assumptions, giving unmatched accuracy and reproducibility. Against this: it is time-consuming, needs repeated breath-holds, and arrhythmia or AF degrades ECG gating and image quality. It is less available than echo, and depends on device compatibility.

🚩 MRI safety. Non-conditional pacemakers and ICDs have historically been a contraindication — though many modern devices are now MR-conditional, so always check the device before scanning. Use gadolinium contrast with caution in renal impairment (nephrogenic systemic fibrosis risk). Severe claustrophobia or an inability to breath-hold also limits or prevents the scan.
🎓 If you need one accurate, repeatable number for the right ventricle or for tracking EF over time, reach for CMR — echo estimates the LV from a geometric assumption, whereas CMR sums real slices (Simpson's) and simply measures it.

Late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) is the workhorse of cardiac MRI tissue characterisation. It answers a clinical question no other test does so elegantly: is a poorly-contracting segment of myocardium dead scar, or living muscle that could wake up if you restore its blood supply? Get the pattern right and you can tell ischaemic scar from non-ischaemic disease, and predict whether revascularisation will actually help.

1The principle — why scar lights up

Gadolinium is an extracellular contrast agent. It cannot cross intact cell membranes, so in normal myocardium — tightly packed living myocytes — there is little extracellular space and it washes out quickly. In acute injury (oedema) and in scar/fibrosis, the extracellular space is expanded and washout is delayed, so gadolinium accumulates and stays behind.

Gadolinium given, then wait ~10 min→contrast has washed out of normal muscle but persists in abnormal tissue

Imaging uses an inversion-recovery sequence with the inversion time set to NULL normal myocardium — healthy muscle is rendered black. Any tissue holding contrast therefore appears BRIGHT (white). The mantra: bright is abnormal.

📷 Image placeholder — describe the cardiac MRI image: a short-axis LGE image with uniformly nulled (black) normal myocardium and a bright white subendocardial rim of enhancement in one wall.
2Viability — reading transmurality

In ischaemic heart disease, infarct scar enhances in a subendocardial or transmural pattern that follows a coronary artery territory (infarction begins at the subendocardium and advances outward as the wavefront progresses). The key number is how far the bright scar extends through the wall thickness — its transmurality.

<25% transmural scar — segment is viable / hibernating; function likely to recover after revascularisation.
25–50% transmural — intermediate; recovery uncertain.
>50% transmural scar — non-viable; function unlikely to recover even if you revascularise.

So LGE directly informs the decision: revascularising a hibernating (viable) but underperfused segment should improve contraction; revascularising dense transmural scar will not. This is its core clinical value in ischaemic cardiomyopathy.

3Pattern recognition — ischaemic vs non-ischaemic

The location of enhancement within the wall is the single most useful discriminator of cause.

🩸Ischaemic (infarct)
Subendocardial or transmural, following a coronary territory. Starts at the endocardium — because that is the last field to be perfused and the first to die.
🫀Non-ischaemic
Mid-wall or epicardial, non-coronary distribution — spares the subendocardium. Seen in cardiomyopathy, myocarditis and infiltration.

Rules of thumb: subendocardial + coronary distribution = ischaemic; mid-wall or epicardial = non-ischaemic. Examples of non-ischaemic patterns include mid-wall stripe in dilated cardiomyopathy, subepicardial enhancement in myocarditis, and patchy/diffuse enhancement in infiltrative disease (e.g. amyloid, sarcoid).

📷 Image placeholder — describe the cardiac MRI image: a side-by-side comparison of subendocardial/transmural enhancement in a coronary territory (ischaemic) versus a mid-wall linear stripe sparing the subendocardium (non-ischaemic cardiomyopathy).
🚩 Gadolinium must be used with caution in severe renal impairment (risk of nephrogenic systemic fibrosis) — check eGFR before contrast. Always confirm MRI device/implant safety (pacemakers, ICDs, certain metallic implants) before scanning.
🎓 LGE turns a wall-motion abnormality into a decision. If a hypocontractile segment shows little or no scar (<25% transmural), it is hibernating myocardium that should recover with revascularisation; if it is more than 50% transmural scar, no bypass or stent will bring it back. Location tells you cause (subendocardial/coronary = ischaemic; mid-wall/epicardial = non-ischaemic), and transmurality tells you prognosis.

Cardiac MRI is the reference standard for characterising the cardiomyopathies because it delivers two things in one study: precise function (volumes, ejection fraction, wall thickness, regional wall motion) and tissue characterisation. The key tissue tool is late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) — gadolinium washes out of normal myocardium but is retained in fibrosis or scar, so the pattern and distribution of LGE tells you both the diagnosis and the prognosis.

📷 Image placeholder — describe the cardiac MRI image.
1The organising principle: LGE pattern localises the disease

Before naming a disease, read where the LGE sits. This single distinction drives most CMR interpretation.

Subendocardial or transmural LGE following a coronary territory→ischaemic pattern (infarct/ischaemic cardiomyopathy)
Mid-wall or epicardial LGE, not respecting coronary territories→non-ischaemic pattern (a cardiomyopathy)

Ischaemic scar advances as a wavefront from the subendocardium outward, so LGE always touches the inner wall. Non-ischaemic fibrosis spares the subendocardium — a crucial way CMR separates a dilated cardiomyopathy from silent coronary disease.

2Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM)

Look for asymmetric septal hypertrophy with a maximal wall thickness ≥15 mm (or ≥13 mm with family history) that is not explained by loading conditions. CMR also demonstrates LVOT obstruction and systolic anterior motion (SAM) of the mitral valve.

Asymmetric septal thickening, septum:posterior-wall ratio typically >1.3
Patchy mid-wall LGE, classically at the RV insertion points and within the hypertrophied septum
Dynamic LVOT gradient with SAM and a posteriorly-directed mitral regurgitation jet

The extent of LGE matters: extensive LGE (>15% of LV mass) flags increased arrhythmia and sudden-death risk and feeds into ICD decision-making alongside the clinical risk score.

2Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) vs ischaemic cardiomyopathy

DCM shows a dilated, globally poorly contracting LV with a low ejection fraction and thinned walls. The characteristic tissue signature is a mid-wall septal stripe of LGE.

Dilated LV, low EF, linear mid-wall septal LGE→DCM with fibrosis — a marker of worse prognosis and arrhythmic risk
Dilated LV, low EF, subendocardial/transmural LGE in a coronary territory→ischaemic cardiomyopathy — refer for revascularisation assessment

This mid-wall vs subendocardial distinction is exactly why CMR is requested when the aetiology of a dilated, failing heart is uncertain.

📷 Image placeholder — describe the cardiac MRI image.
2ARVC and LV non-compaction

Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC) is a disease CMR is uniquely suited to detect, because it is a right-ventricular and regional process.

RV dilatation and dysfunction with reduced RV ejection fraction
Regional RV wall-motion abnormalities, akinetic bulges and aneurysms ("accordion" motion)
RV free-wall thinning and fibrofatty replacement; CMR findings feed the revised Task Force Criteria

LV non-compaction shows prominent, deep trabeculations with a high non-compacted:compacted ratio (>2.3 in diastole on CMR), typically in the apex and lateral wall.

🫀HCM
Asymmetric septum ≥15 mm, SAM/LVOT obstruction, mid-wall LGE at RV insertion points
🎈DCM
Dilated LV, low EF, mid-wall septal stripe of LGE = fibrosis, worse prognosis
⚡ARVC
RV dilatation/dysfunction, fibrofatty replacement, regional aneurysms; Task Force Criteria
🕸️LVNC
Prominent trabeculations, non-compacted:compacted ratio >2.3
🚩 CMR features that predict sudden cardiac death — extensive LGE, severe LV hypertrophy in HCM, and the fibrofatty/aneurysmal RV of ARVC — should prompt ICD referral and risk stratification. Remember safety caveats: gadolinium in severe renal impairment (nephrogenic systemic fibrosis risk) and always confirm MRI-conditional device status before scanning a patient with a pacemaker or defibrillator.
🎓 Read the LGE map like a detective: where the scar sits tells you the diagnosis (subendocardial/coronary = ischaemic; mid-wall or epicardial = cardiomyopathy), and how much scar there is tells you the risk. Function plus tissue characterisation in one scan is why CMR now sits at the centre of cardiomyopathy diagnosis and ICD decision-making.

Myocarditis is inflammation of the myocardium, most often post-viral, and classically presents with chest pain, a raised troponin and ECG changes but unobstructed coronary arteries — a leading cause of MINOCA (myocardial infarction with non-obstructive coronary arteries). Once the angiogram is clean, cardiac MRI (CMR) is the key non-invasive test: it delivers a tissue signature that both confirms inflammation and separates it from a true infarct.

1Recognise the clinical picture

Typically a younger patient, often with a recent viral prodrome (coryzal illness, gastroenteritis), now with acute chest pain, dynamic ECG changes (widespread saddle-shaped ST elevation if perimyocardial, or T-wave changes), and a troponin rise. The invasive angiogram shows unobstructed coronaries — the mismatch that should trigger CMR.

Troponin rise + chest pain + clean coronaries→Think myocarditis (MINOCA) — request cardiac MRI
2The updated Lake Louise Criteria

Diagnosis on CMR rests on two tissue targets — you need one from each pillar. This is the framework to quote in an exam.

Pillar 1 — Myocardial oedema: high signal on T2-weighted imaging and/or raised T2 mapping values, reflecting the water content of acute inflammation.
Pillar 2 — Non-ischaemic injury: late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) in a subepicardial or mid-wall distribution (classically the inferolateral wall), plus raised native T1 and extracellular volume (ECV).
📷 Image placeholder — short-axis post-contrast CMR showing patchy subepicardial/mid-wall LGE in the inferolateral wall, sparing the subendocardium; annotate the non-coronary distribution.
3Myocarditis vs infarct — the discriminator

The distribution of LGE is the single most useful discriminator. Infarction damages tissue from the inside out (the subendocardium is most vulnerable to ischaemia), so its scar hugs the endocardium; inflammation does not respect coronary territories.

🔥Myocarditis
Subepicardial / mid-wall LGE, non-coronary distribution (classically inferolateral). T2 oedema present. Preserved subendocardium.
🩸Infarction
Subendocardial or transmural LGE in a single coronary territory. Follows a vascular pattern, wall-motion abnormality in the same region.
📷 Image placeholder — side-by-side comparison: subendocardial/transmural LGE in a coronary territory (infarct) versus subepicardial LGE (myocarditis).
4Management & course

Most cases are managed with supportive care and treatment of any heart failure; patients are advised to avoid strenuous exercise for several months (exertion during active inflammation risks arrhythmia and sudden death). Pericardial involvement gives perimyocarditis. Most recover fully, but complications include dilated cardiomyopathy, arrhythmia, and — rarely — fulminant myocarditis with cardiogenic shock.

🚩 Fulminant myocarditis — haemodynamic instability, malignant arrhythmia or heart block — is life-threatening and needs urgent cardiology/ICU input and possible mechanical circulatory support. Giant cell myocarditis is an aggressive, rapidly progressive variant. Remember gadolinium caution in significant renal impairment and standard MRI device-safety screening (pacemakers/ICDs, though many modern devices are MR-conditional).
🎓 If troponin is up and the coronaries are clean, the diagnosis lives in the myocardial wall — CMR with the Lake Louise pair (T2 oedema + non-ischaemic LGE) confirms myocarditis, and subepicardial/mid-wall inferolateral LGE is the pattern that tells you it is not an infarct.

Infiltrative and storage cardiomyopathies deposit abnormal material in the myocardium, and cardiac MRI (CMR) is the non-invasive gold standard for characterising them. The workhorses are late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) for scar/deposition patterns and parametric mapping (native T1, T2*, and extracellular volume, ECV) for diffuse tissue change. The pattern of enhancement, the mapping values, and behaviour on the TI (inversion time) scout together point to a specific diagnosis.

1Cardiac amyloidosis — the great myocardial thickener

Amyloid deposits misfolded protein in the interstitium, producing a restrictive cardiomyopathy: biventricular wall thickening (not true hypertrophy), atrial wall thickening, valve thickening, and pericardial/pleural effusions. Systolic function is often preserved until late, but diastolic filling is severely impaired.

Diffuse subendocardial LGE + can't null myocardium on TI scout → think amyloid
LGE: global, often subendocardial (can become transmural) enhancement — not in a coronary territory.
TI scout clue: difficulty nulling the myocardium — the blood pool nulls before or with the myocardium because of abnormal gadolinium kinetics (heavy interstitial amyloid load). A classic exam sign.
Mapping: markedly elevated native T1 and very high ECV (expanded interstitium).

Confirming the subtype matters: ATTR (transthyretin) amyloid is confirmed by bone scintigraphy (DPD/PYP) showing cardiac uptake with negative light chains; AL (light-chain) amyloid needs serum/urine light chains and tissue biopsy, and is treated haematologically.

📷 Image placeholder — describe the cardiac MRI image: 4-chamber LGE showing diffuse global subendocardial enhancement of both ventricles with thickened walls and atrial involvement, plus a TI scout montage where the myocardium fails to null.
2Cardiac sarcoidosis — the patchy mimic

Sarcoid causes non-caseating granulomas that infiltrate the myocardium in a patchy, multifocal way. It classically favours the basal septum and the LV free wall, and the LGE is typically mid-wall or epicardial — again a non-coronary distribution.

Young patient, unexplained high-grade AV block → work up for cardiac sarcoid
LGE: patchy, mid-wall/epicardial, basal septum and free wall predominant.
Clinical triad: conduction disease (AV block), ventricular tachycardia, and heart failure — because granulomas sit in the septum near the conduction system.
FDG PET: complements CMR by detecting active inflammation (guides immunosuppression); CMR LGE reflects established scar.
3Storage diseases mapping picks up — iron and Fabry

Parametric mapping shines where LGE alone would miss diffuse disease.

🧲Iron overload
Haemochromatosis / transfusion-dependent thalassaemia. T2* mapping quantifies myocardial iron: low T2* = high iron (T2* <20 ms abnormal, <10 ms high risk of heart failure/arrhythmia). Guides iron chelation therapy.
🧬Fabry disease
X-linked glycosphingolipid storage. Distinctively LOW native T1 (fat-like lipid lowers T1 — the opposite of amyloid), with basal inferolateral LGE and LVH. A treatable cause with enzyme replacement.

So native T1 direction alone helps: high in amyloid/oedema/fibrosis, low in Fabry (lipid) and iron overload.

📷 Image placeholder — describe the cardiac MRI image: side-by-side native T1 maps and a T2* map — amyloid with elevated T1, Fabry with low T1 basal inferolateral, and an iron-loaded heart with short T2* — plus a short-axis LGE showing patchy mid-wall basal septal sarcoid enhancement.
🚩 Cardiac sarcoid or amyloid presenting with high-grade AV block or ventricular tachycardia carries a real risk of sudden cardiac death. These patients need urgent rhythm assessment and often a pacemaker or ICD — and unexplained AV block in a young person should always prompt a work-up for cardiac sarcoidosis before assuming it is idiopathic.
4Safety housekeeping before you scan

Gadolinium and renal function: check eGFR — gadolinium-based contrast in severe renal impairment risks nephrogenic systemic fibrosis; use group-II macrocyclic agents and weigh risk/benefit. Note ECV calculation requires a haematocrit. Device safety: screen for MRI-conditional status of pacemakers/ICDs, and for other implants; non-conditional devices, certain clips, and metallic foreign bodies may contraindicate the scan or require a specific protocol.

🎓 The single most useful reflex: a non-coronary LGE pattern points to infiltration. Global subendocardial LGE with an un-nullable myocardium and sky-high T1/ECV is amyloid; patchy mid-wall/epicardial basal-septal LGE with AV block or VT is sarcoid; low native T1 flags Fabry or iron. Match the pattern to the biology and the diagnosis follows.

Cardiac MRI is the reference-standard imaging modality for congenital heart disease (CHD), and its role grows across the lifespan — from the adolescent under surveillance to the adult with congenital heart disease (ACHD). Its decisive advantages are no ionising radiation (critical when imaging is repeated for decades), an unrestricted field of view unconstrained by acoustic windows or body habitus, and unrivalled assessment of the right ventricle (RV) — the chamber echocardiography measures worst and the one that most often fails after congenital repair. CMR answers the clinical questions that determine timing of re-intervention: how big and how well-functioning is the RV, how large is the shunt, and what is the anatomy of the great vessels?

1Why CMR over CT or repeat angiography in CHD
CHD patients need imaging repeatedly for life. CMR delivers volumes, function, flow and 3D anatomy in one radiation-free study, so it is preferred over ionising alternatives for serial follow-up. Echocardiography remains first-line in children (bedside, no sedation, portable), and CMR complements — not replaces — it when the RV, great vessels or shunt fraction must be quantified precisely.
Poor echo windows / need for accurate RV volumes→refer for CMR rather than repeat CT angiography
📷 Image placeholder — describe the cardiac MRI image.
2Quantifying the right ventricle — repaired Tetralogy of Fallot
After surgical repair of Tetralogy of Fallot, chronic pulmonary regurgitation (PR) progressively dilates the RV. CMR gives reproducible RV end-diastolic and end-systolic volumes and ejection fraction using a stack of short-axis cines, and phase-contrast flow across the pulmonary trunk gives the regurgitant fraction. Progressive RV dilatation on serial CMR is the principal driver for timing pulmonary valve replacement (PVR) — intervening before the RV becomes irreversibly enlarged or dysfunctional.
Short-axis SSFP cine stack → RV EDV, ESV, EF
Phase-contrast through pulmonary trunk → PR fraction & forward stroke volume
Late gadolinium enhancement → myocardial fibrosis / scar burden
3Shunt quantification — Qp:Qs by phase-contrast flow
In an atrial or ventricular septal defect (ASD/VSD), CMR measures pulmonary flow (Qp) across the pulmonary trunk and systemic flow (Qs) across the aorta directly with phase-contrast velocity mapping. The ratio Qp:Qs quantifies the net left-to-right shunt: a ratio ≥ 1.5:1 indicates a haemodynamically significant shunt that generally warrants closure. This objective number, unavailable from echo alone, guides intervention.
Qp:Qs ≥ 1.5:1 with RV volume overload→significant shunt — consider device/surgical closure
4The great vessels and complex anatomy
CMR maps the great vessels and connections that surgery must plan around: coarctation of the aorta (site, peak gradient across the narrowing, and collateral flow quantified as the difference in aortic flow above vs below the coarct); transposition of the great arteries and its post-operative state after arterial-switch or older atrial-switch (Mustard/Senning) repair; anomalous pulmonary venous drainage; and the single-ventricle / Fontan circulation. Contrast and 3D whole-heart sequences render surgical-planning anatomy without radiation.

🫀RV volumes & function
Reference standard; times PVR in repaired Tetralogy of Fallot with pulmonary regurgitation.
🔀Shunt (Qp:Qs)
Phase-contrast flow in ASD/VSD; ≥ 1.5:1 is significant.
🩸Great vessels
Coarctation gradient/collaterals; transposition & switch anatomy.
☢️No radiation
Enables safe lifelong serial imaging vs repeat CT.
🚩 Severe pulmonary regurgitation with progressive RV dilatation, or a significant left-to-right shunt (rising Qp:Qs) carrying pulmonary hypertension risk and potential shunt reversal (Eisenmenger syndrome), needs specialist ACHD referral for intervention timing. Never forget CMR safety: screen for incompatible devices/implants and assess renal function before gadolinium.
🎓 In congenital heart disease, the recurring exam and clinical question is "how is the right ventricle?" — CMR is the answer because it images the RV, the shunt (Qp:Qs) and the great vessels accurately, repeatedly, and without radiation, making it the modality that dictates the timing of pulmonary valve replacement and shunt closure.
MRI__Hepatobiliary & Abdomen:
Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) is a non-invasive, non-contrast MRI technique that produces a detailed "map" of the biliary tree and pancreatic duct without any cannulation. It exploits the fact that bile and pancreatic juice are static fluids that shine brilliantly on heavily T2-weighted images. Crucially, MRCP is diagnostic only — it tells you who needs the invasive, therapeutic ERCP, sparing everyone else the procedural risks.
1The physics — why fluid glows
MRCP uses a heavily T2-weighted sequence. Static or slow-moving fluid (bile, pancreatic juice, CSF, urine) has a very long T2 relaxation time, so it stays very bright (white), while solid background soft tissue and flowing blood have short T2 and appear dark. The result is a high-contrast image where the fluid-filled ducts stand out like a cholangiogram — but with no contrast agent and no cannulation. No ionising radiation is involved.
Fluid = long T2→bile/pancreatic juice appear bright white; soft tissue dark
📷 Image placeholder — coronal thick-slab T2 MRCP showing the bright fluid-filled biliary tree (right and left hepatic ducts, common hepatic duct, CBD) and pancreatic duct against dark background; gallbladder bright.
2MRCP vs ERCP — the key exam distinction
MRCP is diagnostic and non-invasive. ERCP (endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography) is invasive and therapeutic — an endoscope cannulates the ampulla and allows stone extraction, sphincterotomy and stenting. ERCP carries real risks: post-ERCP pancreatitis (the commonest), perforation, bleeding and cholangitis. The modern pathway therefore uses MRCP first to confirm who has a stone/stricture, so that ERCP is reserved for those who will actually benefit from an intervention.
MRCP = diagnostic, no riskERCP = therapeutic, invasiveImage first, treat second
3What it's used for
Choledocholithiasis — a CBD stone appears as a filling defect (a dark stone within the bright duct). This is the classic workup of obstructive jaundice: gallstones with deranged LFTs (raised ALP/bilirubin) or a dilated CBD on ultrasound. Strictures — malignant (pancreatic head cancer, cholangiocarcinoma) classically give the "double duct sign" = simultaneously dilated CBD and pancreatic duct; benign strictures also assessed. Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) — multifocal "beaded" strictures and dilatations of intra- and extrahepatic ducts, strongly associated with ulcerative colitis. Pancreatic duct anatomy — pancreas divisum, chronic pancreatitis, and IPMN (which communicates with the duct). Also delineates biliary anatomy before surgery.
🪨CBD stone
Dark filling defect in the bright duct; workup of obstructive jaundice.
🎯Double duct sign
Dilated CBD + pancreatic duct → pancreatic head cancer / cholangiocarcinoma.
📿Beaded ducts
Multifocal strictures of PSC; think coexisting ulcerative colitis.
📷 Image placeholder — MRCP showing a dilated CBD with a rounded low-signal filling defect at its distal end (choledocholithiasis) and upstream ductal dilatation.
4MRI safety
As an MRI, the usual safety rules apply. Screen for ferromagnetic implants and devices — older pacemakers/ICDs, cochlear implants, certain aneurysm clips and metallic foreign bodies (e.g. intra-ocular metal) may be contraindications. No iodinated contrast or radiation, so MRCP is well suited to pregnancy and young patients. Practical limits: the patient must lie still and breath-hold, and it is not therapeutic — if intervention is needed, proceed to ERCP.
🚩
Ascending cholangitis is an emergency — don't just image. Suspect it with Charcot's triad (fever, RUQ pain, jaundice); Reynolds pentad adds hypotension and confusion (septic shock). This needs IV antibiotics, resuscitation and urgent biliary drainage (therapeutic ERCP), not merely a diagnostic MRCP. Delaying decompression to obtain imaging in a septic, obstructed patient can be fatal.
🎓 Exam pearl. MRCP is the non-invasive gatekeeper: use it to confirm a CBD stone or stricture and select patients for the invasive, therapeutic ERCP — but in a septic patient with cholangitis, resuscitate and go straight to drainage.

MRI is the single best modality for characterising a focal liver lesion once it has been detected (usually on ultrasound or CT). Its superior soft-tissue contrast, multiphase dynamic post-gadolinium imaging, hepatobiliary-specific contrast agents and diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) let you split lesions into benign vs malignant and read individual lesion signatures — often confidently enough to avoid biopsy.

1Ask the framing question: benign or malignant, and what is the background liver?
The context transforms the differential. In a non-cirrhotic liver, most incidental lesions are benign (haemangioma, cyst, FNH). In a cirrhotic liver, any new arterially-enhancing nodule must be treated as hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) until proven otherwise. Note the number of lesions too: solitary favours a primary process, multiple favours metastases.
2Learn the sequences that do the characterising work
T2-weighted: fluid and haemangiomas are very bright; solid tumours are mildly bright.
Dynamic post-gadolinium (arterial, portal-venous, delayed phases): shows the enhancement pattern over time — the core of characterisation.
Hepatobiliary phase (gadoxetate / Gd-EOB-DTPA): taken up by functioning hepatocytes ~20 min after injection; helps detect small mets and distinguish FNH from adenoma.
Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI): restricted diffusion favours malignancy (dense, cellular tissue).
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image: axial T2-weighted liver showing a well-defined, markedly hyperintense ("light bulb" bright) segment VI lesion typical of a haemangioma, alongside darker background liver parenchyma.
3Match the benign lesion signatures
💡Haemangioma
Commonest benign liver lesion. Very bright on T2 ("light bulb"), with peripheral nodular discontinuous enhancement that fills in centripetally (edge → centre) on delayed images.
⭐Focal nodular hyperplasia (FNH)
Benign hyperplastic response. Central scar, homogeneous arterial enhancement, and retains hepatobiliary contrast (contains functioning hepatocytes and bile ductules) — the key to separating it from adenoma.
💊Hepatic adenoma
Linked to oestrogens (OCP) and anabolic steroids. Does not retain hepatobiliary contrast. Matters because of the risk of bleeding and malignant transformation — may need resection.
💧Simple cyst
Very bright on T2, low on T1, sharply marginated and no enhancement after contrast. Benign, no follow-up needed.
4Recognise the malignant patterns
Cirrhotic liver + arterial hyperenhancement with portal-venous/delayed washout and an enhancing capsule→Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). This LI-RADS signature is diagnostic — HCC can be diagnosed on imaging alone, without biopsy.
Multiple lesions, known primary (esp. colorectal), often hypovascular with peripheral rim enhancement and restricted diffusion→Metastases — the commonest malignant liver lesion overall. Hepatobiliary-phase imaging improves detection of small deposits.
Infiltrative mass with capsular retraction, progressive delayed enhancement and upstream biliary dilatation→Cholangiocarcinoma.

Diffusion restriction favours malignancy across all of these — a quick discriminator when the enhancement pattern is equivocal.

📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image: dynamic post-gadolinium series in a cirrhotic liver showing a segment VIII nodule with brisk arterial-phase hyperenhancement followed by portal-venous washout and a peripheral enhancing pseudocapsule — the diagnostic imaging signature of HCC.
🚩 A new arterially-enhancing lesion with washout in a cirrhotic liver is HCC until proven otherwise — do not dismiss it. Refer to the HCC MDT and continue 6-monthly surveillance imaging in at-risk cirrhotics. Separately, gadolinium contrast requires caution in severe renal impairment (historic risk of nephrogenic systemic fibrosis), and standard MRI safety screening applies (pacemakers, ferromagnetic implants, cochlear devices).
🎓 Think in two axes: background liver (cirrhotic vs normal) and enhancement over time. Peripheral nodular fill-in = haemangioma; central scar that retains hepatobiliary contrast = FNH; arterial enhancement + washout + capsule in cirrhosis = HCC (biopsy not required); multiple hypovascular lesions with restricted diffusion = mets. Contrast dynamics plus DWI do most of the diagnostic work.

MRI can non-invasively quantify two things that used to demand a liver biopsy: fat (steatosis, NAFLD/MASLD) and iron (haemochromatosis, transfusional overload). Both exploit how protons behave in different chemical/magnetic environments — and, crucially, fat and iron cause signal loss on opposite echo images.

1Fat — chemical shift imaging (in-phase vs out-of-phase / Dixon)

Fat and water protons precess at slightly different frequencies. At certain echo times their signals add (in-phase); at others they cancel (out-of-phase). A voxel containing both fat and water therefore loses signal on out-of-phase images (the shorter TE at 1.5T).

Voxel loses signal on OUT-of-phase image→intracellular fat present (steatosis)
India-ink / etching artefact: a dark line outlining fat–water interfaces (organ borders) on out-of-phase images — the signature of chemical shift.
PDFF (proton density fat fraction): multi-echo Dixon sequence giving a quantitative % liver fat, used to grade and monitor NAFLD/MASLD and as a trial endpoint.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image: paired in-phase and out-of-phase axial images; liver signal drops markedly on the out-of-phase image with India-ink etching at organ margins, confirming diffuse steatosis.
2Iron — T2*/R2* mapping

Iron is paramagnetic: it creates local field inhomogeneity that rapidly dephases protons, shortening T2* (and T2). A high-iron liver therefore loses signal as TE lengthens — darkest on longer-echo (in-phase) images.

Liver darkens on longer-TE / IN-phase image→iron overload — quantify with T2*/R2* mapping

R2* (= 1/T2*) is calibrated to give the liver iron concentration (LIC), guiding venesection in hereditary haemochromatosis and iron chelation in transfusion-dependent thalassaemia.

3The key trap — fat and iron behave OPPOSITELY

This is the classic exam discriminator. Watch which echo the signal drops on:

💧Fat
Signal drops on OUT-of-phase (shorter TE). Steatosis / NAFLD-MASLD. Quantified by PDFF (%).
🧲Iron
Signal drops on IN-phase (longer TE). Overload / haemochromatosis. Quantified by T2*/R2* → LIC.
🪢Fibrosis
MR elastography (MRE) maps tissue stiffness to stage fibrosis — a stiff liver suggests advanced fibrosis/cirrhosis.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image: a T2*/R2* parametric map of the liver colour-coded for iron, with an ROI over the right lobe showing markedly shortened T2* and a raised LIC value consistent with iron overload.
4Why it matters clinically

NAFLD/MASLD is very common and tracks with metabolic syndrome (obesity, T2DM, dyslipidaemia). It can progress: simple steatosis → steatohepatitis (NASH) → fibrosis → cirrhosis → HCC. Serial PDFF lets you monitor response to weight loss and therapy without repeat biopsy.

Hereditary haemochromatosis (usually HFE C282Y homozygosity) drives iron deposition causing cirrhosis, diabetes ("bronze diabetes"), cardiomyopathy, arthropathy and hypogonadism. Quantifying LIC and de-ironing (venesection) before organ damage sets in is disease-modifying.

🚩 Cirrhosis from either fat or iron mandates HCC surveillance (6-monthly ultrasound ± AFP). Iron also loads the heart — cardiac T2* assesses myocardial iron and cardiomyopathy/arrhythmia risk, the leading cause of death in transfusion overload. And remember MRI safety: screen for ferromagnetic implants, non-conditional pacemakers, cochlear implants and metallic foreign bodies before scanning.
🎓 One-liner: fat drops out on OUT-of-phase, iron drops in on IN-phase. PDFF quantifies fat, R2*/T2* quantifies iron (LIC), MRE quantifies fibrosis — together replacing biopsy for grading and monitoring diffuse liver disease.

An adrenal incidentaloma is a lesion found on imaging done for another reason — it is common (found on ~5% of abdominal CTs, rising with age). Two questions decide management: Is it functioning? (biochemistry) and Is it benign or malignant? (imaging). MRI chemical shift imaging is the key MRI tool for the second question — it exploits intracytoplasmic (microscopic) lipid to confirm the commonest benign lesion, the lipid-rich adrenal adenoma.

1The two questions for every incidentaloma

Never read the imaging in isolation. Every adrenal nodule prompts a hormonal work-up to exclude a functioning lesion, and a characterisation pathway to exclude malignancy.

Functioning?→Cortisol/overnight dexamethasone (Cushing's), aldosterone:renin (Conn's), plasma/urinary metanephrines (phaeochromocytoma)
Benign or malignant?→Size, morphology, and lesion characterisation — CT density/washout or MRI chemical shift
2The chemical shift principle

Fat and water protons precess at slightly different frequencies. At certain echo times their signals are in-phase (add together) and at others out-of-phase / opposed-phase (cancel each other). Where fat and water coexist within the same voxel — as with the microscopic intracytoplasmic lipid of an adenoma — the out-of-phase image shows signal loss. This is the same physics that makes a fatty liver drop signal out-of-phase.

In-phase (IP): fat + water signals add — adenoma appears bright/normal.
Out-of-phase (OOP): fat + water cancel — lipid-rich adenoma drops signal (goes darker) versus IP.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image: paired in-phase and out-of-phase (opposed-phase) axial images of the same right adrenal nodule; the nodule is bright on the in-phase image and visibly darker on the out-of-phase image, confirming a lipid-rich adenoma.
3Interpreting the signal drop
Signal drops OOP→Lipid-rich benign adenoma — reassure, no further imaging follow-up needed for the characterisation question
No signal drop→Lipid-poor / indeterminate — could be lipid-poor adenoma, phaeochromocytoma, metastasis, or adrenocortical carcinoma; needs CT washout or further work-up

Chemical shift is very good at the positive call (drop = benign adenoma) but a lack of drop does not equal malignant — roughly 30% of adenomas are lipid-poor and will not lose signal. That group joins the indeterminate pathway rather than going straight to surgery or biopsy.

4Imaging signatures of the non-adenoma lesions
💡Phaeochromocytoma
Very T2 bright ("light-bulb" sign), avidly enhancing, may have cystic/necrotic areas. No OOP drop. Biochemistry: raised metanephrines.
🎯Metastasis
Often bilateral, in a patient with a known primary (lung, breast). Lipid-poor, no OOP drop.
⚠️Adrenocortical carcinoma
Large (often >4–6 cm), heterogeneous, necrosis/haemorrhage, irregular margins. Grows on follow-up.
🟡Myelolipoma
Benign, contains macroscopic fat (follows fat on all sequences, drops with fat saturation). Chemical shift may show India-ink etching only at fat–soft-tissue interfaces.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image: T2-weighted axial showing a markedly hyperintense ("light-bulb bright") left adrenal mass consistent with a phaeochromocytoma, with no signal loss on the out-of-phase sequence.
5MRI safety and correlation

Standard MRI safety applies: screen for ferromagnetic implants, pacemakers/ICDs, cochlear implants, intraocular metal fragments; check renal function before gadolinium (risk of nephrogenic systemic fibrosis in severe renal impairment). Always feed the imaging back into the clinical picture — correlate with the hormonal work-up before deciding on surgery or surveillance.

🚩 Never biopsy or operate on a suspected phaeochromocytoma before alpha-blockade. An unblocked phaeo can be tipped into a life-threatening hypertensive crisis by biopsy, surgery, or contrast. Manage with alpha-blockade first, then beta-blockade (never beta before alpha — unopposed alpha vasoconstriction). A large, heterogeneous mass with necrosis raises the possibility of adrenocortical carcinoma and should not be assumed benign.
🎓 Signal drop out-of-phase = lipid-rich benign adenoma — the single highest-yield MRI adrenal fact. If it does not drop, it is indeterminate, not automatically malignant: think lipid-poor adenoma, phaeo (T2 light-bulb, metanephrines), metastasis (known primary), or ACC (large/heterogeneous) — and pursue CT washout plus the hormonal work-up.

MR enterography (MRE) is the preferred cross-sectional imaging test for small-bowel Crohn's disease. It uses no ionising radiation — decisive in young patients who will need repeated scans across a lifetime — and shows the full thickness of the bowel wall and everything beyond the reach of the colonoscope. It is complementary to ileocolonoscopy: the scope inspects the mucosa and takes biopsies, MRE assesses transmural and extraluminal disease and its complications.

1Get the technique right — you cannot read collapsed bowel

A negative test on poorly distended bowel is worthless. The protocol is built to open the small bowel out and freeze it.

Oral (luminal) contrast: a large volume of a mannitol/water-based solution drunk over ~45–60 min. Mannitol is a non-absorbed sugar alcohol that holds fluid in the lumen (osmotic) to distend the bowel — it is bright on T2, dark on T1 ("biphasic").
Antiperistaltic agent: IV hyoscine butylbromide (Buscopan) — or glucagon — given to paralyse peristalsis and abolish motion blur.
IV gadolinium: post-contrast T1 fat-saturated sequences reveal mucosal hyperenhancement — the key marker of active inflammation.
Core sequences: T2 (± fat sat) for oedema, T1 pre/post gadolinium, and diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) for restricted diffusion in inflamed segments.
Bowel loops collapsed / poorly filled→non-diagnostic — inflammation can be masked or mimicked; ensure adequate oral prep before reporting
📷 Image placeholder — coronal T2 MR enterogram showing a well-distended small bowel filled with bright luminal fluid, with a segment of thickened, narrowed terminal ileum.
2Recognise the signs of active inflammation

Active Crohn's produces a cluster of findings centred on the terminal ileum, classically with skip lesions (diseased segments separated by normal bowel).

Mural thickening — wall >3 mm; the single most consistent finding.
Mucosal hyperenhancement — avid post-gadolinium enhancement of the inner wall; layered/stratified ("mural stratification") enhancement suggests active disease.
Mural oedema — the wall is T2 bright (best on fat-saturated T2); a direct sign of active inflammation.
DWI restriction — high signal on high b-value DWI with low ADC in the inflamed segment.
Comb sign — engorged, closely spaced vasa recta radiating perpendicular to the inflamed loop, like the teeth of a comb; reflects mesenteric hyperaemia.
Fibrofatty proliferation / "creeping fat" — mesenteric fat wrapping around the diseased bowel; a marker of chronicity.
📷 Image placeholder — post-gadolinium fat-saturated T1 image of the terminal ileum showing avid mucosal hyperenhancement, mural thickening, and the comb sign of engorged vasa recta in the adjacent mesentery.
3Active inflammation vs chronic fibrosis — this changes management

The clinician's central question is whether a narrowed segment is driven by active inflammation (treat medically — biologics/steroids) or fixed fibrosis (may need surgery/endoscopic dilatation). MRE is the best non-invasive way to tell them apart.

Wall enhancement + T2 oedema + DWI restriction→predominantly active — escalate medical therapy
Stricture with little enhancement, no oedema, low T2 signal→predominantly fibrotic — medication won't reverse it; consider surgery/dilatation

In practice strictures are often mixed; reporting the degree of enhancement guides the balance of treatment.

4Complications — what makes the report urgent
⛔Stricture
Luminal narrowing with pre-stenotic dilatation (>3 cm) upstream. Inflammatory vs fibrotic distinction drives medical vs surgical care.
🔀Fistula
Abnormal tract: entero-enteric, enterocutaneous, enterovesical, or perianal. May form a stellate "asterisk" of tethered loops.
🫧Abscess
Rim-enhancing fluid collection, often DWI-restricting, ± gas. Contraindicates biologics — needs drainage/antibiotics first.
➰Sinus tract
Blind-ending track from the bowel wall into the mesentery — a precursor to fistula/abscess; signals transmural penetrating disease.

Perianal fistulising disease is imaged with a dedicated MRI pelvis (perianal fistula protocol) to map tracks and collections before surgery.

5MRI safety — never skip the checklist

Before any MRI, screen for ferromagnetic hazards: older/non-conditional pacemakers and ICDs, cochlear implants, intracranial aneurysm clips, and metallic intra-ocular foreign bodies (metalworkers). Ask about implants and give a gadolinium allergy and renal history — gadolinium is linked to nephrogenic systemic fibrosis in severe renal impairment. Buscopan is contraindicated in untreated angle-closure glaucoma and used with caution in significant cardiac disease.

🚩 An obstructing stricture (colicky pain, vomiting, abdominal distension, dilated proximal loops) or an abscess / perforation with sepsis is an emergency needing urgent surgical/GI input, not an outpatient follow-up. Flag perianal fistulising disease and any collection promptly, as it changes management and delays biologic therapy.
🎓 When you read an MR enterogram, answer three questions the gastroenterologist actually cares about: Where is the disease (terminal ileum? skip lesions?), how active is it (enhancement + T2 oedema + DWI = medical treatment), and are there complications (stricture with pre-stenotic dilatation, fistula, abscess = possible surgery). Distension is everything — a report on collapsed bowel is not a normal report.

MRI of the kidneys is the problem-solver of uroradiology: it characterises renal masses and cysts without ionising radiation, and it excels at local staging of renal cell carcinoma (RCC) — above all the cranial extent of venous tumour thrombus. Reach for it when CT or ultrasound is indeterminate, or when iodinated contrast and radiation are best avoided (young patients, pregnancy, or the need for repeated follow-up).

1When to choose MRI over CT/US

MRI is a second-line, problem-solving tool. Its multiparametric sequences (T1, T2, chemical-shift, diffusion, dynamic post-gadolinium) distinguish benign from malignant lesions and, crucially, map disease extent for the surgeon.

Indeterminate renal lesion on CT/US→multiparametric MRI to characterise
Avoid radiation/iodinated contrast (young, pregnant, repeated follow-up)→MRI preferred
Known RCC needing surgical planning→MRI to define tumour thrombus extent
2RCC — the mass and local staging

A solid, enhancing renal mass is RCC until proven otherwise. MRI answers the mass characterisation question, but its unique value is local staging: perinephric spread, nodal disease, and — most importantly — venous tumour thrombus.

Solid mass showing avid enhancement after gadolinium
Tumour thrombus extending into renal vein and IVC
MRI defines the cranial extent of IVC thrombus (infrahepatic vs retrohepatic vs supradiaphragmatic/atrial)
Perinephric fat stranding and enlarged regional nodes

The cranial level of thrombus dictates the surgical approach — infrahepatic thrombus is managed differently from thrombus reaching the right atrium (which may require cardiopulmonary bypass). This is where MRI directly changes the operation.

📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image: coronal post-gadolinium T1 showing an enhancing right renal mass with tumour thrombus filling the renal vein and extending cranially up the IVC, arrow marking the superior extent.
3Cyst characterisation — the Bosniak classification

The Bosniak system stratifies cystic renal lesions by malignant potential. The single most important malignant feature is enhancement of septa or walls/nodules after contrast.

IBosniak I
Simple cyst — thin wall, no septa, no enhancement. Clearly benign, no follow-up.
IIBosniak II / IIF
Minimally complex — few thin septa or fine calcification. II benign; IIF ("follow-up") needs surveillance imaging.
IIIBosniak III
Thickened, irregular, enhancing walls/septa. Surgical — significant malignant risk.
IVBosniak IV
Enhancing soft-tissue nodule/solid component. Likely malignant — surgical.

MRI is more sensitive than CT for detecting subtle septal enhancement, making it valuable for equivocal (IIF/III) lesions.

4Angiomyolipoma (AML) — hunting fat

AML is a benign tumour containing macroscopic fat. On MRI, fat loses signal on fat-suppressed sequences and shows India-ink etching at fat–water interfaces on chemical-shift/opposed-phase imaging — the diagnostic clue.

Signal drop-out on fat-suppression confirms macroscopic fat
Multiple bilateral AMLs → think tuberous sclerosis
Large AMLs (>4 cm) carry a risk of spontaneous haemorrhage

Note the caveat: fat-poor AMLs can mimic RCC, and rarely RCC contains fat, so an entirely fat-free "AML" still warrants caution.

📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image: paired in-phase and opposed-phase T1 images of a renal lesion, with signal drop-out and India-ink boundary artefact confirming macroscopic fat in an angiomyolipoma.
5Complex cysts, ADPKD and gadolinium safety

Haemorrhagic/proteinaceous cysts are bright on T1 and can be confidently called benign on MRI when they show no enhancement. In autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD), MRI measures total kidney volume — the key imaging prognostic marker for disease progression — and MRA can screen for intracranial berry aneurysms where indicated (family history, symptoms).

ADPKD prognostication→MRI total kidney volume
ADPKD + relevant history→MRA to screen for berry aneurysm

Gadolinium caution: in severe renal impairment (eGFR <30) and dialysis patients, gadolinium-based agents carry a risk of nephrogenic systemic fibrosis (NSF) — a particularly relevant hazard in this renal population. Use macrocyclic (group II) agents and weigh the indication carefully.

🚩 An enhancing complex cyst (Bosniak III/IV) or any solid enhancing renal mass is likely RCC — refer to urology. The cranial extent of IVC tumour thrombus directly alters the surgical approach and must be reported. A large angiomyolipoma may rupture, causing life-threatening retroperitoneal haemorrhage (Wunderlich syndrome). Never scan a patient with an MRI-unsafe implant, and avoid gadolinium in severe renal impairment/dialysis because of NSF risk.
🎓 Enhancement is the currency of renal MRI: septal or nodular enhancement upgrades a cyst toward malignancy (Bosniak III/IV), avid solid enhancement flags RCC, and absence of enhancement lets you confidently call a complex/haemorrhagic cyst benign. Fat that drops out on fat-suppression means angiomyolipoma. And remember the two safety reflexes unique to the renal patient — MRI implant screening, and no gadolinium in advanced renal failure.
MRI__Pelvis:
Multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) of the prostate is now performed before biopsy in men with suspected prostate cancer (raised PSA or abnormal DRE). It can spare men an unnecessary biopsy and, when biopsy is needed, lets the urologist target the suspicious area rather than sampling blindly. Read it in three sequences, score it with PI-RADS, then stage the tumour.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image: axial T2-weighted image showing prostate zonal anatomy, with a lentiform low-signal focus in the left peripheral zone.
1Know the sequences and what each shows
mpMRI combines anatomical and functional imaging. T2-weighted shows zonal anatomy — the peripheral zone (PZ, normally high T2 signal) versus the central transition zone (TZ). Prostate cancer in the PZ appears as low T2 signal (a rounded/lentiform dark focus). Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI/ADC) is the most important sequence for peripheral-zone cancer — tumour is densely cellular, so water diffusion is restricted (high signal on high-b DWI, low signal on the ADC map). Dynamic contrast enhancement (DCE) with gadolinium shows early/rapid enhancement of tumour and is used as a tie-breaker.
T2 → zonal anatomy; PZ cancer = low signal
DWI/ADC → restricted diffusion; dominant for PZ
DCE → early enhancement (tie-breaker)
2Score it with PI-RADS v2.1
Findings are scored PI-RADS 1–5 (1 = very low, 5 = very high likelihood of clinically significant cancer). The dominant sequence depends on location: DWI drives the score in the peripheral zone, whereas T2 drives the score in the transition zone. A score of ≥3–4 usually prompts a targeted (MRI-fusion) biopsy, while PI-RADS 1–2 may allow biopsy to be safely avoided. This up-front triage is what reduces unnecessary biopsies.
PI-RADS 4 lesion in peripheral zone→MRI-fusion targeted biopsy + MDT discussion
3Stage the tumour locally (T stage)
mpMRI also provides local staging, which changes management. Look for extracapsular extension (bulging/breach of the capsule), seminal vesicle invasion, and involvement of the neurovascular bundle. Organ-confined disease may allow nerve-sparing prostatectomy; extracapsular or seminal-vesicle disease pushes towards radiotherapy or non-nerve-sparing surgery. This T-staging guides the surgery-versus-radiotherapy decision at MDT.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image: ADC map with a focal dark (low-ADC) lesion corresponding to restricted diffusion in the right peripheral zone, confirming a suspicious focus.
4Distinguish benign mimics and look for spread
Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) arises in the transition zone and produces well-defined nodules ("organised chaos") — do not over-call these as cancer. Prostate cancer characteristically metastasises to bone, where deposits are typically sclerotic (osteoblastic). Bone spread is assessed with a bone scan or whole-body MRI, not routine mpMRI of the pelvis alone.
🎯Peripheral-zone cancer
Low T2 signal + restricted diffusion (DWI/ADC dominant). PI-RADS driven by DWI.
🧩Transition-zone / BPH
Well-defined nodules; T2 is the dominant sequence here. Do not over-call BPH.
🦴Bone metastases
Sclerotic deposits; assess with bone scan or whole-body MRI.
🚩
A high PI-RADS lesion (≥4) needs a targeted biopsy and MDT discussion — do not simply reassure. Separately, spinal cord compression from prostate bone metastases is an oncological emergency: new back pain with neurology needs urgent whole-spine MRI and immediate dexamethasone. Remember MRI safety — screen for pacemakers, ferromagnetic implants and metallic foreign bodies, and check renal function before gadolinium.
🎓 Exam pearl. In the peripheral zone, DWI/ADC is the dominant sequence and cancer restricts diffusion; in the transition zone, T2 is dominant. mpMRI before biopsy allows both avoidance of unnecessary biopsies and MRI-fusion targeting of PI-RADS ≥3–4 lesions.

Ultrasound is the first-line imaging test for gynaecological disease. MRI pelvis is the problem-solving modality: it is called on when ultrasound is equivocal, when a mass is complex, or when the surgeon needs an anatomical map before myomectomy, uterine artery embolisation (UAE) or excision of deep endometriosis. Its superb soft-tissue contrast — especially on T2 — lets you separate fibroids, adenomyosis and endometriosis with confidence.

1Fibroids (leiomyomas) — mapping for surgery

Fibroids are benign smooth-muscle tumours. On MRI they are well-defined, low (dark) T2 signal masses, sharply demarcated from adjacent myometrium. MRI's job is to count them and locate each one, because location dictates treatment.

Sharply-marginated dark-T2 uterine mass→Leiomyoma — report number, size and FIGO location
Submucosal — bulges into the cavity; causes menorrhagia and subfertility; suits hysteroscopic resection.
Intramural — within the myometrial wall; the commonest type.
Subserosal / pedunculated — projects outward on a stalk; can mimic an adnexal mass.
Degeneration — outgrows its blood supply; red degeneration in pregnancy causes acute pain and peripheral T1-bright signal.

MRI plans myomectomy vs UAE: it confirms viable enhancing fibroids suitable for embolisation and excludes pedunculated subserosal lesions (relative UAE contraindication).

📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image: sagittal T2 uterus showing a well-defined low-signal submucosal fibroid indenting the endometrial cavity, with a separate intramural fibroid in the posterior wall.
2Adenomyosis — the junctional zone mimic

Adenomyosis is endometrial glands within the myometrium. Unlike the discrete fibroid, it is diffuse: MRI shows thickening of the junctional zone >12 mm with small T2-bright foci and an ill-defined, globular ("boggy") uterus. Clinically — menorrhagia, dysmenorrhoea and a tender bulky uterus.

◈Fibroid
Focal, sharply-marginated dark-T2 mass; a discrete lump you can shell out.
▦Adenomyosis
Diffuse junctional-zone thickening >12 mm with tiny bright foci; ill-defined margins.
3Endometriosis — endometriomas and deep disease

MRI is the key tool for characterising ectopic endometrial tissue, and for mapping deep infiltrating endometriosis (DIE) before surgery.

T1-hyperintense cyst that does NOT drop out on fat-saturation→Endometrioma ("chocolate cyst") — blood products, with T2 shading
Endometrioma — T1 hyperintense (old blood) that stays bright on fat-sat, with dependent T2 shading; distinguishes it from a dermoid (fat suppresses) or haemorrhagic cyst.
Deep disease sites — pouch of Douglas, uterosacral ligaments, rectovaginal septum, bladder and bowel wall; seen as T2-dark fibrotic nodules with tethering/distortion.
Surgical map — MRI defines depth, ureteric and bowel involvement so the MDT can plan excision and warn about resection risk.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image: axial T1 fat-saturated image showing a bright right ovarian endometrioma that fails to suppress, alongside a T2-dark nodule tethering the posterior vaginal fornix in the pouch of Douglas.
4Müllerian anomalies & MRI safety

MRI is the reference standard for congenital uterine anomalies, distinguishing a septate uterus (normal convex fundal contour, fibrous septum — hysteroscopically correctable) from a bicornuate uterus (fundal cleft >1 cm indenting the outer contour) — a distinction that changes fertility management.

Safety: MRI uses no ionising radiation, but screen every patient for ferromagnetic implants, pacemakers and cochlear devices; gadolinium is generally avoided in pregnancy.

🚩 Features suggesting malignancy — a rapidly growing, complex or solid-enhancing adnexal mass, or thick irregular septations — must be characterised and referred to gynae-oncology. Severe deep endometriosis with ureteric or bowel involvement (hydronephrosis, stricture) needs formal MDT planning, not routine excision.
🎓 The three-way split is the exam favourite: a fibroid is a focal dark-T2 mass, adenomyosis is diffuse junctional-zone thickening >12 mm, and an endometrioma is T1-bright that will not fat-suppress. Reach for MRI when ultrasound cannot answer the question or the surgeon needs a map.

MRI is the workhorse for local staging of gynaecological cancers of the uterus and cervix. Its superior soft-tissue contrast makes it the imaging tool of choice for mapping tumour size, depth of invasion and spread into adjacent structures — the data that steers the gynae-oncology MDT between surgery and chemoradiotherapy. FIGO staging for both cervical and endometrial cancer now incorporates imaging and surgical findings, and MRI is central to that assessment.

📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image. Sagittal T2 pelvis: cervical tumour of intermediate-high signal expanding the cervix, seen against the low-signal fibrous cervical stroma; annotate the intact low-signal stromal ring.
1Cervical cancer — what MRI answers
Cervical cancer is usually squamous cell carcinoma and HPV-related. On T2-weighted imaging the tumour is intermediate-to-high signal and stands out against the normally low-signal fibrous cervical stroma. MRI assesses:
Tumour size and depth of stromal invasion.
Parametrial invasion — the pivotal question. The intact low-signal stromal ring around the tumour excludes parametrial spread; disruption of that ring with tumour extending into parametrial fat signals invasion.
Vaginal extension (upper vs lower third), and bladder or rectal wall involvement.
Pelvic sidewall involvement and hydronephrosis.
Pelvic and para-aortic lymph nodes.
Loss of the low-signal cervical stromal ring with tumour in parametrial fat→Parametrial invasion — moves the patient from primary surgery to chemoradiotherapy
2Endometrial cancer — what MRI answers
Endometrial cancer is an adenocarcinoma and classically presents with postmenopausal bleeding. The single most important MRI measurement is the depth of myometrial invasion:
<50% vs ≥50% myometrial invasion — the key prognostic and staging factor, and the finding that guides whether lymphadenectomy is performed. Deep (≥50%) invasion carries higher nodal risk.
Cervical stromal involvement — upstages disease and alters surgical extent.
Serosal breach, adnexal spread and pelvic/para-aortic nodal disease.
Dynamic contrast-enhanced sequences help distinguish tumour from normal myometrium and sharpen the depth-of-invasion call.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image. Sagittal T2 uterus: endometrial tumour distending the cavity with a tumour front extending more than halfway through the myometrium; annotate the ≥50% depth of invasion against the outer myometrial margin.
3Where MRI sits in the pathway
MRI findings feed the gynae-oncology MDT and complement the rest of the workup rather than replacing it.
🔬Tissue diagnosis
Cervical biopsy / colposcopy; endometrial biopsy (pipelle) or hysteroscopy for the histological diagnosis.
🩺EUA
Examination under anaesthesia assesses clinical extent, vaginal and parametrial spread alongside MRI.
🖥️CT / PET-CT
Screens for distant metastatic disease and distant nodal spread that MRI of the pelvis does not cover.
📡TVUS
First-line for postmenopausal bleeding — endometrial thickness triages who needs biopsy.
🚩 Postmenopausal bleeding is endometrial cancer until proven otherwise and must always be investigated — transvaginal ultrasound for endometrial thickness followed by biopsy/hysteroscopy. Watch for advanced disease presenting with hydronephrosis (sidewall/ureteric involvement) or a vesicovaginal or rectovaginal fistula. On MRI safety: screen every patient for pacemakers and incompatible implants, ferromagnetic foreign bodies and pregnancy, and use gadolinium contrast cautiously in renal impairment.
🎓 One line to remember each cancer: for cervical cancer MRI is really asking "is the low-signal stromal ring intact?" — because parametrial invasion means chemoradiotherapy, not surgery; for endometrial cancer MRI is asking "is myometrial invasion <50% or ≥50%?" — because depth of invasion drives lymphadenectomy. T2 is the key sequence for both.
High-resolution MRI is the gold standard for LOCAL staging of rectal cancer. It is not just descriptive imaging — it directly decides who receives neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy before surgery and whether the surgeon can achieve a clear total mesorectal excision (TME). The single most important question the MRI answers is: is the mesorectal fascia (the circumferential resection margin) safe?
📷 Image placeholder — axial T2-weighted MRI of the mid rectum showing the tumour, the surrounding fatty mesorectum, and the thin dark line of the mesorectal fascia (MRF) enveloping it. Annotate the shortest distance from tumour edge to MRF.
1The mesorectum, MRF and CRM — the decisive relationship
The mesorectum is the fatty envelope around the rectum containing lymph nodes and vessels; it is bounded by a thin fascial layer, the mesorectal fascia (MRF). In TME surgery the MRF is the plane of dissection, so it becomes the circumferential resection margin (CRM). On MRI, measure the shortest distance from tumour (or an involved node or tumour deposit) to the MRF.
Tumour/node/EMVI ≤1 mm from MRF→threatened / involved CRM → neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy to downstage before TME
MRF appears as a fine low-signal (dark) line on T2.
A clear CRM (>1 mm) predicts a low local recurrence rate.
2T-stage — depth of invasion through the wall layers
T2-weighted images resolve the rectal wall layers. The key threshold is breach of the muscularis propria.
①T1 / T2
Confined to the wall (submucosa / muscularis propria intact). Often surgery alone.
②T3
Through muscularis into perirectal fat. Substaged by depth of extramural spread (mrT3a–d).
③T4
Invades adjacent organs (T4b) or breaches peritoneum (T4a). Needs neoadjuvant therapy.
3EMVI and nodal staging — the prognostic markers
Extramural venous invasion (EMVI) is tumour signal expanding and extending along a perirectal vein beyond the muscularis. It is an independent poor prognostic marker — higher risk of distant metastasis and often pushes toward neoadjuvant treatment. For nodes, morphology beats size: suspicious features are an irregular/spiculated border, mixed heterogeneous signal, and round shape — a small node with these features is more concerning than a large smooth one.
EMVI: tubular tumour signal tracking along a vessel, with vessel expansion.
Tumour deposits in the mesorectum also count toward CRM assessment.
📷 Image placeholder — coronal T2 MRI of a low rectal tumour showing its relationship to the levator ani and the intersphincteric plane, illustrating the decision point between sphincter-sparing anterior resection and abdominoperineal resection.
4Low rectal tumours, restaging and distant staging
For low tumours, MRI defines the relationship to the anal sphincter complex and levators: this decides sphincter-sparing anterior resection versus abdominoperineal resection (APR) with a permanent stoma. After neoadjuvant therapy, MRI is repeated to assess response using the MRI tumour regression grade (mrTRG) — fibrosis versus residual tumour signal. Distant staging (liver, lung) is done by CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, not by pelvic MRI.
Low tumour reaching intersphincteric plane / levators→APR rather than sphincter-preserving resection
🚩 A threatened/involved CRM (≤1 mm) or T4 disease converts management to neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy before any surgery — reporting these accurately is the whole point of the scan. An obstructing tumour is a surgical emergency and cannot wait for elective staging pathways. Always confirm MRI safety first: screen for pacemakers, ferromagnetic implants, cochlear implants and metallic foreign bodies before the patient enters the scanner.
🎓 Remember the four numbers/letters that change the plan on a rectal MRI report: CRM (≤1 mm = threatened), T-stage (T3 through muscularis, T4 into organs), EMVI (present = poor prognosis), and the height/sphincter relationship. Nodes are judged by morphology, not size. MRI stages local disease and drives neoadjuvant decisions; CT covers distant metastases.

MRI of the pelvis using a dedicated anal fistula protocol is the gold standard for mapping perianal fistulae before surgery. It defines the primary tract, its relationship to the anal sphincter complex, any secondary tracts or abscesses, and the internal opening — the information a surgeon needs to cure the fistula without causing incontinence.

1Why MRI, and what it answers

A perianal fistula is an abnormal epithelialised track between the anal canal (internal opening) and the perianal skin (external opening). Surgery fails and recurs when a tract or extension is missed, and incontinence results when too much sphincter is divided. MRI maps all of this pre-operatively.

Recurrent or complex fistula→MRI to find the missed tract, extension or undrained abscess
Primary tract — course from internal to external opening.
Sphincter relationship — how much internal/external sphincter it crosses.
Secondary extensions — horseshoe tracts, supralevator spread, abscess.
Internal opening — usually at the dentate line (site of anal glands).
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image: axial T2 of the anal canal showing the internal sphincter, external sphincter and a bright fluid-filled intersphincteric tract, with the internal opening at the dentate line.
2Sequences: what makes the tract light up

The protocol combines high-resolution anatomy with fluid- and inflammation-sensitive sequences.

T2 / STIR — an active, fluid-filled tract is bright (high signal); STIR suppresses fat to make it stand out.
Post-gadolinium (T1 fat-sat) — enhancing granulation tissue lining the wall of an active tract; a fibrotic/inactive tract enhances little.
Small field-of-view, thin slices angled to the anal canal for sphincter detail.
3Parks classification

Parks classifies fistulae by the relationship of the primary tract to the sphincters — this drives the operation.

1Intersphincteric
Commonest. Tract runs in the intersphincteric plane, crossing only the internal sphincter.
2Transsphincteric
Crosses both internal and external sphincter into the ischioanal fossa.
3Suprasphincteric
Loops up over puborectalis/levators before descending — high, complex.
4Extrasphincteric
Bypasses the sphincter entirely, rectum to skin — think Crohn's, trauma or pelvic sepsis.

Practically, fistulae are also graded simple (low, single tract, crossing little sphincter) versus complex (high transsphincteric/supra-/extrasphincteric, multiple tracts, horseshoe, abscess, anterior in women, or Crohn's).

📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image: coronal STIR showing a transsphincteric tract crossing the external sphincter with a horseshoe extension arcing posteriorly through the deep postanal space.
4Aetiology and the Crohn's link

Most fistulae are cryptoglandular — an infected anal gland at the dentate line drains, forms an abscess, and tracks out. The key association to flag on MRI is Crohn's disease.

Multiple, complex or recurrent fistulae with proctitis→Think perianal Crohn's — needs medical + surgical MDT

Perianal Crohn's typically produces complex, branching or multiple tracts and needs biologics/immunomodulators alongside conservative surgery (setons rather than aggressive cutting).

5Surgical relevance: how much sphincter?

The single most important MRI output is how much sphincter the tract crosses, because that decides the operation and the incontinence risk.

Low / minimal sphincter — can be laid open (fistulotomy) safely.
High / much sphincter, complex, Crohn's — sphincter-preserving: seton, LIFT (ligation of intersphincteric tract) or advancement flap.
Identify the internal opening and any horseshoe extension so nothing is left undrained.
🚩 A perianal abscess or spreading anorectal sepsis is a clinical diagnosis needing urgent incision and drainage — do not wait for MRI. In the diabetic or immunocompromised patient, necrotising perineal sepsis (Fournier's gangrene) is a surgical emergency. Consider underlying Crohn's or malignancy in atypical or recurrent fistulae. Standard MRI safety applies — screen for pacemakers, ferromagnetic implants and gadolinium contraindications (renal impairment, pregnancy).
🎓 On MRI, a bright T2/STIR fluid tract that enhances after gadolinium is active; the report should always state the Parks type, how much sphincter is crossed, the internal opening and any secondary extension — that quartet is what the surgeon operates on.

Ultrasound (transvaginal) is the first-line test for an ovarian/adnexal mass. When US is indeterminate — a lesion that is not confidently benign nor obviously malignant — MRI is the best problem-solving test. It uses tissue signatures (fat, blood, fibrous tissue, fluid) plus dynamic contrast enhancement, reported through the O-RADS MRI risk system, to sort masses into benign vs malignant and guide whether the patient needs a gynae-oncology referral.

1Why MRI — the problem-solving role

MRI does not replace ultrasound; it characterises the mass US could not classify. Its power is superb soft-tissue contrast: it can prove the presence of macroscopic fat, blood products, or dense fibrous tissue, and can show whether solid areas enhance after gadolinium (a marker of viable, vascularised — potentially malignant — tissue).

T1 — fat and blood are bright.
Fat-saturation / chemical shift — confirms macroscopic fat (drops out) vs blood (stays bright).
T2 — fluid is bright; fibrous tissue is very dark.
Dynamic post-gadolinium — enhancing solid tissue = the worrying finding.

Results are scored with the O-RADS MRI system (score 1 = normal → 5 = high probability of malignancy), directly linking imaging appearance to malignancy risk and onward management.

2Benign tissue signatures — the reassuring look

Certain benign lesions have diagnostic MRI fingerprints that let you avoid surgery:

💧Simple cyst
Uniformly T2 bright, T1 dark, thin wall, no enhancing solid component. Benign functional cyst.
🩸Endometrioma
T1 hyperintense that does NOT suppress on fat-sat (blood, not fat); low signal on T2 = “T2 shading”. “Chocolate cyst”.
🧈Mature cystic teratoma (dermoid)
Contains macroscopic fat — T1 bright that drops on fat-sat / chemical-shift. May show a Rokitansky nodule.
🪨Fibroma / fibrothecoma
Solid but very low T2 (dense fibrous tissue). Benign; may cause Meigs syndrome (mass + ascites + pleural effusion).
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image: paired axial T1 and T1 fat-saturated images of an adnexal lesion that stays bright on both (endometrioma, blood) contrasted with a dermoid whose bright T1 signal drops out on fat-sat.
T1 bright that suppresses on fat-sat→macroscopic fat = dermoid
T1 bright that does NOT suppress + T2 shading→blood = endometrioma
3Malignant features — favouring epithelial ovarian cancer

The features that push O-RADS up and suggest malignancy reflect viable, invasive tumour and spread:

Large size and predominantly solid composition.
Enhancing solid / vascular components (avid dynamic enhancement).
Thick, irregular enhancing septa and papillary projections.
Necrosis within solid tissue.
Ascites, peritoneal deposits and omental cake — signs of dissemination.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image: axial post-contrast T1 fat-saturated pelvic MRI showing a large complex adnexal mass with an avidly enhancing solid mural nodule, thick irregular septa and surrounding ascites.
Complex mass + enhancing solid tissue + ascites→ovarian malignancy until proven otherwise
4From MRI to management

MRI stratifies risk and plans the patient's route: confidently benign signatures can be managed conservatively or with simple surgery, while indeterminate or O-RADS 4–5 lesions are referred to the gynae-oncology MDT. In advanced disease, CT (chest/abdomen/pelvis) is added to complete staging and assess resectability.

RMI (Risk of Malignancy Index) = US features × menopausal status × CA-125, used clinically alongside imaging to triage referral.
MRI safety — screen for pacemakers/incompatible implants and metallic foreign bodies before scanning; the strong magnetic field is a projectile hazard.
Gadolinium caution in renal impairment (nephrogenic systemic fibrosis) — check eGFR.
🚩 A complex, solid, enhancing adnexal mass with ascites is ovarian malignancy until proven otherwise — refer to the gynae-oncology MDT. Separately, sudden severe pelvic pain with an enlarged, oedematous ovary suggests ovarian torsion, a surgical emergency needing urgent operative assessment.
🎓 US finds the mass; MRI characterises it by tissue signature. Learn the three fingerprints — fat that suppresses = dermoid, blood that won't suppress + T2 shading = endometrioma, very dark T2 solid = fibroma — and treat enhancing solid tissue, thick irregular septa/papillary projections and ascites as the O-RADS red flags that send the patient down the malignancy pathway.
MRI__Breast:
Contrast-enhanced (dynamic gadolinium) breast MRI is the most sensitive imaging test for breast cancer. It is used for annual surveillance of high-risk women, in whom mammography alone is inadequate — particularly the dense, radiographically difficult breasts of younger women. It detects cancers by their abnormal blood supply, not by their density or calcification, which is why it outperforms mammography and ultrasound for sensitivity.

1Why MRI, and the underlying principle

Invasive cancers are angiogenic — they recruit a leaky, disorganised neovasculature to fuel growth. After intravenous gadolinium, malignant lesions show rapid, avid enhancement followed by washout. This dynamic behaviour, not anatomy alone, is what MRI exploits.

No ionising radiation — safe for young women and for repeated annual imaging.
Sees through dense fibroglandular tissue that obscures mammographic cancers.
Detects multifocal / contralateral disease missed by other modalities.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image: axial post-contrast T1 fat-saturated breast MRI showing an avidly enhancing irregular spiculated mass in the upper outer quadrant against suppressed background parenchyma.
2Who is screened — the high-risk groups

MRI surveillance is reserved for women whose lifetime risk is high enough that mammography alone would miss too much. NICE-defined eligible groups include:

🧬BRCA1 / BRCA2
Known carriers, and untested first-degree relatives of a carrier.
⚠️TP53 / Li-Fraumeni
Very high penetrance; screened from a young age.
👪Strong family history
High lifetime risk on NICE family-history criteria without a known gene.
☢️Prior chest radiotherapy
Mantle / chest RT when young, e.g. Hodgkin lymphoma survivors.
Young + dense breasts + high genetic risk→annual MRI, usually alongside mammography
3Interpreting the scan — dynamic curves and BI-RADS

Enhancement over time is plotted as a dynamic (kinetic) curve and the lesion is categorised using BI-RADS:

Type 1 — progressive/persistent enhancement: usually benign.
Type 2 — plateau: indeterminate.
Type 3 — rapid uptake then washout: the classic suspicious/malignant pattern.

Morphology matters too: irregular spiculated masses and clumped/segmental non-mass enhancement are suspicious, whereas smooth homogeneous rounded lesions are more often benign.

📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image: time–signal intensity kinetic curves showing a type 3 curve (steep early rise then washout, red line) contrasted with a benign type 1 persistent curve (green line).
4Limitations and practical protocol

The trade-off for outstanding sensitivity is lower specificity. Benign tissue enhances too, generating false positives, extra recalls and biopsies, plus patient anxiety.

Pre-menopausal woman→scan days 7–14 of cycle to reduce background parenchymal enhancement
Expensive and resource-intensive relative to mammography.
Requires intravenous gadolinium contrast every time.
Standard MRI safety screen: pacemakers, ferromagnetic implants, cochlear implants, claustrophobia.
🚩 A suspicious enhancing lesion is not a diagnosis — it mandates triple assessment (clinical exam, imaging, and image-guided biopsy) before any treatment. Exercise gadolinium caution in renal impairment (risk of nephrogenic systemic fibrosis; check eGFR), and always complete the MRI safety checklist before scanning.
🎓 Remember the trade: breast MRI is the most sensitive but least specific mainstream breast test — brilliant for finding cancer in high-risk young dense breasts, but it over-calls benign enhancement. Use it for surveillance of high-risk women alongside mammography, time it to the follicular phase (days 7–14), and read the type 3 washout curve as the hallmark of malignancy.
