Breast cancer is diagnosed by triple assessment (clinical exam + mammography/US + core biopsy) — MRI plays no part in making the diagnosis. Once cancer is confirmed, contrast-enhanced breast MRI becomes a selective local-staging and problem-solving tool: it maps disease extent, hunts for additional foci, and answers specific surgical questions. It is not a routine test for every new cancer, and its findings must be interpreted alongside — never instead of — mammography, US and histology.

1Know MRI's place: problem-solving, not first-line

The diagnosis is already made before MRI is considered. MRI is requested to refine surgical planning when a specific question exists. Its great strength is sensitivity for invasive disease; its weakness is modest specificity, so benign lesions also enhance.

Cancer confirmed on biopsy, surgical plan unclear→Selective contrast-enhanced MRI to define extent
Dynamic gadolinium sequences show malignant enhancement (early rapid uptake, washout kinetics).
High sensitivity for invasive cancer; extent often mapped more accurately than on mammography.
Lower specificity — incidental benign enhancement is common and can mislead.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image: axial post-gadolinium subtracted T1 showing an irregular enhancing index tumour in the upper outer quadrant with spiculated margins.
2The recognised indications (why MRI is added)

Each indication exists because MRI changes the operation — wide local excision versus mastectomy, or the timing of surgery.

🧭Extent & multifocality
Detects additional ipsilateral (multifocal/multicentric) or contralateral cancers that alter surgical planning.
🔬Invasive lobular carcinoma
Often mammographically occult and size-underestimated; MRI defines true extent far better.
🧱Chest wall / pectoral
Assesses posterior tumours for pectoral muscle or chest wall invasion.
💧Neoadjuvant response
Monitors and measures residual tumour before and after neoadjuvant chemotherapy.
🕵️Occult primary
Axillary nodal metastasis with no primary on mammography/US — MRI may find it.
📏Size discrepancy
Resolves conflict between clinical and conventional imaging estimates of tumour size.
3Understand the downside: overestimation & overtreatment

Because MRI is highly sensitive but only moderately specific, it can overestimate disease and pick up incidental benign enhancement. This triggers extra biopsies and can push patients toward more extensive surgery or unnecessary mastectomy — without proven survival benefit. Hence its judicious, question-driven use.

MRI shows an unexpected extra enhancing lesion→Biopsy it — do not change the operation on imaging alone
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image: a second small enhancing focus in a different quadrant from the index tumour (potential multicentric disease), flagged for second-look ultrasound and targeted biopsy.

MRI complements mammography, US and biopsy — it never replaces them. It is also a valuable adjunct in high-risk screening, but as a staging tool it is deployed selectively.

🚩 An MRI-detected additional lesion must be histologically confirmed (usually by second-look US and targeted core biopsy) before escalating surgery. Never convert a planned wide local excision to a mastectomy on the basis of MRI enhancement alone — incidental benign enhancement is common.

Safety essentials: MRI needs intravenous gadolinium contrast — check renal function (eGFR) given the (small) risk of nephrogenic systemic fibrosis in severe impairment. Apply standard MRI safety screening: pacemakers/implants, ferromagnetic devices, cochlear implants, and metallic foreign bodies. The examination is prone position with dedicated breast coils; timing in premenopausal women is ideally days 7–14 of the cycle to reduce background parenchymal enhancement.

🎓 MRI in breast cancer answers a surgical question, it does not make the diagnosis. Reserve it for defining extent, invasive lobular carcinoma, chest wall involvement, neoadjuvant response, occult primary, or size discrepancy — then confirm any new lesion with biopsy before letting it change the operation.

MRI is the single best test for assessing the integrity of a silicone breast implant. It uses silicone-specific (silicone-selective / water-suppressed) sequences and needs no contrast to answer the question “is the implant ruptured?”. It is used for routine surveillance of certain implants and to work up symptomatic patients (pain, lump, or a change in breast shape).

1Know the normal implant anatomy

A silicone implant is a silicone gel filling held inside a thin silicone shell (the elastomer envelope). The body then lays down a fibrous capsule around the shell. On MRI you should be able to trace an intact shell sitting just inside its fibrous capsule.

Wavy low-signal infoldings of the shell→Radial folds — a NORMAL finding, not rupture

Radial folds are normal invaginations of the shell into the gel; do not mistake them for the linguine sign.

📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image.
2Intracapsular rupture — the linguine sign

In intracapsular rupture the silicone shell fails but the leaking gel stays contained within the intact fibrous capsule. The collapsed, floppy shell floats freely inside the pool of silicone.

Linguine sign — multiple wavy, low-signal curvilinear lines (the collapsed shell) suspended in silicone. This is the classic, near-pathognomonic MRI sign of intracapsular rupture.
Keyhole / teardrop / noose sign — a droplet of silicone tracking into a radial fold; an early sign of shell failure while the shell is only partly collapsed.
Wavy low-signal lines within silicone, capsule intact→Intracapsular rupture (linguine sign)
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image.
3Extracapsular rupture — silicone escapes

In extracapsular rupture both the shell AND the fibrous capsule are breached, so silicone escapes beyond the capsule into the surrounding breast tissue and can migrate to axillary lymph nodes. Free silicone collections form siliconomas (silicone granulomas).

Silicone-signal foci outside the capsule / in nodes→Extracapsular rupture
4Other findings to name
🪞Capsular contracture
Thickened, tightened fibrous capsule making the implant firm, rounded and painful; may distort shape.
💧Gel bleed
Microscopic silicone seepage through an INTACT shell — a small amount of silicone just outside the shell without frank rupture.
🧪Saline vs silicone
Saline implants follow water signal and collapse/deflate visibly when they rupture; silicone rupture needs dedicated silicone sequences.
5BIA-ALCL and MRI safety

BIA-ALCL (breast implant-associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma) is a rare T-cell lymphoma linked to textured implants. It classically presents with a late (>1 year) peri-implant seroma or a mass. Management starts with ultrasound-guided aspiration of the fluid sent for cytology and CD30; it is NOT diagnosed on the implant integrity scan alone.

MRI safety: confirm the patient is safe to scan (implanted devices, pacemakers) and remember most breast implants themselves are MRI-conditional/safe — the safety check is about the whole patient, not the implant.

🚩 A new late peri-implant seroma or mass is not “just rupture” — you must exclude BIA-ALCL: aspirate the fluid and send it for CD30 and cytology. Symptomatic or extracapsular rupture may require surgical explant.
🎓 Linguine = intracapsular (collapsed shell floating, capsule intact); silicone outside the capsule = extracapsular. Silicone rupture needs no contrast — just silicone-specific sequences. And any late peri-implant effusion means think BIA-ALCL and send fluid for CD30.

A woman presents with a firm axillary lymph node. Core biopsy shows metastatic adenocarcinoma with ER/PR positivity and GATA3 expression — a breast phenotype — yet mammography and ultrasound of both breasts are normal. This is the classic occult breast primary: the disease has declared itself in a node while the primary tumour hides. Contrast-enhanced breast MRI is the key next investigation, finding the mammographically and sonographically invisible cancer in the majority of these patients so it can be biopsied, localised and treated with breast conservation.

1Recognise the presentation
Metastatic adenocarcinoma in an axillary node (occasionally supraclavicular or a distant site) with no palpable or imaged breast mass. Histology and immunohistochemistry point to breast origin: ER/PR positive, GATA3 positive, and consideration of HER2 status. In a woman, axillary nodal adenocarcinoma is an occult breast primary until proven otherwise.
2Confirm conventional imaging is negative
Bilateral mammography and whole-breast ultrasound (including the axilla) are performed first. When both are normal but the nodal disease has a breast phenotype, the primary is occult to standard imaging — the trigger for MRI.
Node biopsy = breast-type adenocarcinoma + normal mammogram/US→arrange contrast-enhanced breast MRI
3Contrast-enhanced breast MRI — the high-yield test
Gadolinium-enhanced MRI is highly sensitive for invasive breast cancer and detects the occult primary in the majority of cases where mammography and US are negative. The primary typically appears as an enhancing mass — often with irregular margins and washout kinetics — or as a focus of non-mass enhancement.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image.
Irregular enhancing mass with rapid uptake and washout → suspicious primary
Segmental/clumped non-mass enhancement → possible DCIS or invasive component
Enlarged, rounded axillary nodes with loss of fatty hilum → nodal disease
4Target the lesion — second-look US or MRI-guided biopsy
Once MRI shows a candidate, arrange a second-look ultrasound aimed at the enhancing area; if seen, biopsy under US. If sonographically occult, perform MRI-guided biopsy and place a marker clip for later surgical localisation.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image.
5Why finding the primary changes management
Locating the tumour converts an "unknown primary" into a treatable breast cancer. It permits breast-conserving surgery and targeted therapy rather than empirical whole-breast radiotherapy or mastectomy given when no primary is found, and refines staging and adjuvant decisions. MRI also helps in Paget's disease of the nipple with an occult underlying cancer, and when clinical and conventional imaging findings are discordant regarding disease extent.
🧬Occult breast primary
Nodal breast-type adenocarcinoma; normal mammogram/US; MRI finds it — biopsy and conserve.
🎗️Paget's with occult cancer
Nipple change, normal mammogram — MRI maps underlying DCIS/invasive disease.
⚖️Discordant findings
Clinical and imaging extent disagree — MRI clarifies true disease burden before surgery.
🚩 Axillary nodal adenocarcinoma in a woman is an occult breast primary until excluded. If mammography and ultrasound are negative, do contrast-enhanced breast MRI and refer urgently to the breast MDT — do not label it a carcinoma of unknown primary without a breast MRI.

Remember MRI safety and gadolinium considerations: screen for MRI-incompatible implants and devices; check renal function before gadolinium and avoid group-1 (high-risk) agents in severe renal impairment because of nephrogenic systemic fibrosis; and ask about pregnancy. Breast MRI is best timed in the second week of the menstrual cycle (days 7–14) to minimise background parenchymal enhancement that can obscure a small primary.

🎓 In carcinoma of unknown primary, immunophenotype localises the source and imaging finds the lesion: ER/PR/GATA3-positive nodal adenocarcinoma in a woman says "breast", and contrast-enhanced MRI is the test that turns an occult primary into a resectable, breast-conservable cancer.
MRI__Vascular (MRA / MRV):
Intracranial MR angiography (MRA) maps the Circle of Willis and the major cerebral arteries — most often WITHOUT contrast, using a clever trick called time-of-flight. It is the workhorse for elective aneurysm screening and for looking at intracranial stenosis, dissection and vascular malformations.

1How it works — time-of-flight (TOF)

The commonest intracranial MRA technique is time-of-flight (TOF). Stationary tissue in the imaging slab is repeatedly hit with radiofrequency pulses and becomes saturated (dark). Blood flowing into the slab is fresh and unsaturated, so it appears bright. Contrast between bright flowing blood and dark background creates the angiogram — no gadolinium needed.

Flowing (unsaturated) blood enters the slab→high signal (bright) against saturated dark tissue = the vessel map

Images are reconstructed into rotating maximum-intensity-projection (MIP) views so the Circle of Willis can be inspected from all angles.

📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRA image: TOF MIP of a normal Circle of Willis, showing bright anterior cerebral, middle cerebral and posterior cerebral arteries with the communicating vessels, on a dark suppressed background.
2What we use it for

Key indications for intracranial MRA:

Aneurysm detection/screening. Berry (saccular) aneurysms cluster at arterial branch points — anterior communicating artery, posterior communicating artery, and the MCA bifurcation. MRA is used for elective screening in ADPKD, strong family history (≥2 affected first-degree relatives), and surveillance after treated subarachnoid haemorrhage.
Stenosis / occlusion. Intracranial atherosclerosis in ischaemic stroke work-up, and characteristic patterns such as moyamoya (progressive supraclinoid ICA narrowing with a hazy collateral network).
Other vasculopathy. Arterial dissection, vasculitis (beaded/irregular calibre), and arteriovenous malformations / feeding vessels.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRA image: TOF MRA showing a saccular outpouching at the anterior communicating artery region (aneurysm), with an inset comparing a normal branch point.
3Where MRA sits vs CT/DSA — modality shortlist

Match the clinical question to the right test. For an acute presentation the pathway is NOT MRA first.

🧲MRA (TOF)
Elective aneurysm screening/follow-up, stenosis, dissection, vasculitis. No radiation, no contrast.
💻CT angiography
Fast and highly sensitive for aneurysm; the first angiographic test in acute SAH after non-contrast CT head.
🎯DSA
Digital subtraction angiography — gold standard for characterising aneurysms AND the platform for endovascular coiling.
Suspected acute SAH (thunderclap headache)→non-contrast CT head → CTA / DSA — not MRA
4Pitfalls & MRI safety
TOF overestimates stenosis. Turbulent or slow flow causes signal loss (dephasing), so a stenosis can look tighter — or a near-occlusion look complete — than it truly is. Confirm with CTA/DSA when it will change management.
Motion sensitive. Long acquisition means movement degrades the study; small distal or slow-flow aneurysms may be missed.
MRI safety. Screen for pacemakers/ICDs, cochlear implants, ferromagnetic foreign bodies (e.g. intra-ocular metal), and certain aneurysm clips. TOF needs no contrast, avoiding gadolinium concerns.
🚩 Thunderclap headache — sudden "worst-ever" headache peaking within seconds is subarachnoid haemorrhage until proven otherwise. Do an urgent non-contrast CT head; if negative and within window, lumbar puncture (xanthochromia) and CT angiography. This is a neurosurgical emergency — refer for coiling/clipping. Do not reach for an elective MRA in this setting.
🎓 TOF-MRA is the non-contrast Circle-of-Willis screen: bright flowing blood, no gadolinium, ideal for elective aneurysm surveillance (ADPKD, family history) and intracranial stenosis. But it flatters stenoses and lags the acute pathway — remember that a ruptured aneurysm is worked up by CT then CTA/DSA, and an incidental unruptured aneurysm goes to the neurovascular MDT to weigh size and site against treatment risk.

MRA of the carotid and neck images the extracranial carotid and vertebral arteries. Its two headline jobs at medical-school level are grading carotid artery stenosis after a TIA or ischaemic stroke, and diagnosing carotid or vertebral artery dissection — the classic cause of stroke in the young.

1Carotid stenosis in the stroke work-up

After a TIA or ischaemic stroke, the key surgical question is: is there significant stenosis of the carotid on the symptomatic side (ipsilateral to the ischaemic event)? Atherosclerotic plaque at the carotid bifurcation is a source of thromboembolism to the brain. Duplex ultrasound is usually first-line; MRA (or CTA) confirms and grades the stenosis before any intervention.

Symptomatic carotid stenosis ≥50–70% (NASCET)→refer for carotid endarterectomy (or stenting) to prevent recurrent stroke
Stenosis quantified by NASCET criteria — narrowest lumen vs the normal distal ICA diameter.
Endarterectomy benefit is greatest done urgently, within ~2 weeks of the event.
Asymptomatic or contralateral stenosis carries far less benefit from surgery.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRA image: contrast-enhanced MRA of the neck showing a tight focal stenosis at the origin of the right internal carotid artery with post-stenotic narrowing, compared to the widely patent contralateral vessel.
2Carotid & vertebral artery dissection

Dissection is a leading cause of stroke in the young. It follows neck trauma or manipulation (including chiropractic/sports) or arises spontaneously, often with an underlying connective tissue disorder (e.g. Ehlers-Danlos, Marfan, fibromuscular dysplasia). Blood tracks into the vessel wall forming an intramural haematoma.

Fat-saturated T1 shows a bright crescent in the vessel wall→"crescent sign" of intramural haematoma (methaemoglobin) = dissection
Crescent sign — bright methaemoglobin in the wall on fat-saturated T1.
Luminal narrowing / flame-shaped taper or a "string sign" on MRA.
Carotid dissection can cause a painful Horner's syndrome (partial — ptosis + miosis, sparing sweating).
3Technique & MRI safety
🧲TOF MRA
Time-of-flight — no contrast; relies on flowing blood. Can overestimate stenosis where flow is turbulent or slow.
💉CE-MRA
Contrast-enhanced (gadolinium) — faster, less flow-dependent, generally more accurate for grading stenosis and the great vessels.
⚠️Safety
Screen for pacemakers, ferromagnetic implants, cochlear implants; caution with gadolinium in severe renal impairment (NSF risk).
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRA image: axial fat-saturated T1 of the neck showing a bright crescentic intramural haematoma surrounding a narrowed left internal carotid lumen, the classic crescent sign of dissection.
🚩 A patient with a TIA or minor stroke and ≥50–70% symptomatic carotid stenosis needs urgent referral for carotid endarterectomy within 2 weeks — delay wastes the window of maximal benefit. In a young stroke patient, suspect dissection and treat urgently with antiplatelet or anticoagulation; do not dismiss neck pain plus Horner's syndrome.
🎓 Match the imaging to the question: ipsilateral (symptomatic) side and NASCET grade decide endarterectomy; a bright crescent on fat-sat T1 in a young patient decides dissection. Ultrasound screens, MRA/CTA confirms.
MR venography (MRV) maps the dural venous sinuses and is the go-to test for cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST) — a stroke-type emergency that loves to hide behind a headache. Learn to spot the missing sinus and to keep anticoagulating even when the brain has bled.
1What MRV shows and when to order it

MRV demonstrates flow within the superior sagittal, transverse, sigmoid and straight sinuses and the deep venous system. It is the key investigation whenever you suspect CVST. The positive finding is absent flow / a filling defect in a sinus that should light up.

New severe or progressive headache + seizure / focal signs / raised ICP → think CVST → urgent MRV (or CT venography)
Absent flow-related signal in a sinus that normally opacifies = the core MRV sign of thrombosis.
Correlate with plain MRI: loss of the normal flow void and abnormal signal within the sinus.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRV image: 2D time-of-flight MRV with non-visualisation / abrupt cut-off of the left transverse and sigmoid sinus, contrasted with the normally opacified right side.
2How CVST presents

Headache is the commonest symptom — it may be thunderclap or slowly progressive. Other pictures: raised ICP (papilloedema, visual blurring/obscurations), seizures, and focal neurological deficits.

A venous infarct does not respect arterial territories — it crosses arterial boundaries and is frequently haemorrhagic. A bleed that ignores vascular territory in a young or peripartum patient should make you reach for MRV.

Parasagittal haemorrhagic infarct crossing an arterial boundary → suspect superior sagittal sinus thrombosis.
Bithalamic oedema/infarction → suspect deep (internal cerebral vein / straight sinus) thrombosis.
3Risk factors — think prothrombotic

CVST is a clotting problem, so hunt for a prothrombotic driver:

🤰Pregnancy / puerperium
Hypercoagulable state; classic peripartum trigger.
💊COCP
Combined oral contraceptive pill — a common young-woman risk factor.
🧬Thrombophilia
Factor V Leiden, antiphospholipid, etc.
💧Dehydration
Haemoconcentration / sluggish venous flow.
🎗️Malignancy
Paraneoplastic hypercoagulability.
🦠Local infection
Mastoiditis / sinusitis → adjacent sinus thrombosis.
4Signs on CT / MRI / MRV

Beyond the MRV filling defect, know the plain-imaging clues:

Empty delta sign — non-enhancing thrombus surrounded by enhancing dura in the superior sagittal sinus on contrast CT/MRI.
Cord sign — hyperdense thrombosed cortical vein/sinus on non-contrast CT.
Loss of the normal flow void on MRI, with abnormal signal in the sinus and restricted diffusion (DWI) in the clot/infarct.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRV image: post-contrast axial showing the empty delta sign — a triangular non-enhancing filling defect within the enhancing walls of the superior sagittal sinus.
5Management

The treatment is anticoagulation (therapeutic LMWH or unfractionated heparin), even when there is venous haemorrhagic infarction — you are treating the clot, and the bleed is a consequence of the venous obstruction, not a contraindication.

Confirmed CVST, including with haemorrhagic infarct → anticoagulate (LMWH/heparin); investigate for the underlying prothrombotic cause

Beware over-calling: a hypoplastic or atretic transverse sinus is a common normal variant and can mimic thrombosis on MRV. Look for a small bony jugular foramen, absence of thrombus signal, and correlate with plain MRI before diagnosing.

🚩 CVST is a stroke-type emergency. A new severe or persistent headache with seizures, focal signs or raised ICP — especially in a pregnant or COCP-using woman — demands urgent MRV (or CTV) and prompt anticoagulation. Do not be reassured by a "normal" CT; venous infarcts and early thrombus are easily missed.
🚩 MRI safety: screen every patient before scanning — pacemakers/implanted devices, ferromagnetic aneurysm clips, cochlear implants, metallic foreign bodies (especially intra-ocular), and pregnancy/gadolinium considerations must all be checked before the patient enters the magnet.
🎓 Whenever you see a haemorrhagic infarct that crosses arterial territories in a young woman on the pill or just postpartum, say "venous" and order the MRV — then anticoagulate the clot even if it has already bled.

Magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) images the renal arteries without ionising radiation. In the renal patient its chief job is to hunt for renal artery stenosis (RAS) — a treatable cause of secondary hypertension and progressive renal impairment.

1When to suspect RAS

MRA is requested when the clinical picture points away from simple essential hypertension. The classic triggers cluster around resistant blood pressure and unexpected renal responses to blockade of the renin-angiotensin system.

Creatinine jumps >30% after starting an ACE inhibitor/ARB→think significant RAS (often bilateral)
Resistant hypertension (uncontrolled on 3+ agents) or accelerated/malignant hypertension.
Hypertension presenting in the young, or new severe hypertension after age 55.
Recurrent "flash" pulmonary oedema with preserved LV function.
An abdominal or flank bruit on auscultation.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRA image: coronal contrast-enhanced MRA of the abdominal aorta and both renal arteries, showing a tight focal narrowing at the ostium of the right renal artery with post-stenotic dilatation.
2Two causes, two patterns

Recognising the pattern on MRA points to the cause, which in turn dictates management. Atherosclerosis and fibromuscular dysplasia sit at opposite ends of the demographic and anatomical spectrum.

🫀Atherosclerotic RAS
Commonest cause (~90%). Older patients with vascular risk factors. Plaque at the ostium/proximal third of the artery. Often coexists with coronary and peripheral disease.
📿Fibromuscular dysplasia
Young women. Affects the mid/distal artery. Classic "string of beads" appearance from alternating stenoses and dilatations. Non-atherosclerotic, responds well to angioplasty.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRA image: mid-to-distal right renal artery of a young woman showing the alternating narrowings and outpouchings of the classic "string of beads" appearance of fibromuscular dysplasia.
3Why it drives blood pressure — and how we treat it

Reduced renal perfusion beyond the stenosis is sensed by the juxtaglomerular apparatus, which releases renin and activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS). The result is angiotensin-II-driven vasoconstriction and aldosterone-driven sodium retention — renovascular hypertension. MRA demonstrates the stenosis and any post-stenotic dilatation.

Medical therapy is the mainstay — RAAS blockade (with monitoring), plus statin, antiplatelet and risk-factor control.
Angioplasty ± stent for selected cases — FMD responds particularly well to plain angioplasty.
Revascularisation in atherosclerotic RAS gives limited added benefit over medical therapy in randomised trials; reserve for refractory hypertension, deteriorating function or flash oedema.
🚩 In severe renal impairment, gadolinium contrast risks nephrogenic systemic fibrosis (NSF) — a real hazard in this very population. Use newer lower-risk agents, non-contrast MRA techniques, or an alternative modality, and always check the eGFR before contrast.
🎓 Bilateral RAS (or RAS in a single functioning kidney) plus an ACE inhibitor/ARB can precipitate acute kidney injury, because efferent arteriolar tone is what maintains filtration pressure. Remember MRI safety too — screen every patient for pacemakers, ferromagnetic implants and metal foreign bodies before the scanner. And in any young hypertensive, actively look for the "string of beads" of FMD.
Contrast-enhanced MR angiography (CE-MRA) maps the arterial tree from the aorta down to the pedal vessels — the lower-limb "run-off" — without ionising radiation or iodinated contrast. It is the radiation-free alternative to CT angiography and catheter DSA for planning revascularisation in peripheral arterial disease.
1What it shows and how it is done
A bolus of gadolinium is tracked as it passes down the aorta and into the legs, acquired in stations from the diaphragm to the feet. The result is a continuous "run-off" map of the arterial tree: aorta → common/external iliacs → common femoral → superficial femoral (SFA) → popliteal → the crural trifurcation (anterior tibial, posterior tibial, peroneal) → pedal arches. It demonstrates the SITE of stenosis or occlusion, its LENGTH, and the collateral pathways that reconstitute vessels distally.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRA image: coronal maximum-intensity-projection run-off from aorta to feet, showing a short focal occlusion of the left superficial femoral artery with reconstitution of the popliteal via geniculate collaterals.
2Peripheral arterial disease — localising the level
MRA classifies disease into three levels that drive treatment choice:
Short focal stenosis / occlusion→endovascular angioplasty ± stent
Long-segment occlusion, good distal run-off→surgical bypass
Aortoiliac — buttock/thigh claudication, may impair erection (Leriche syndrome).
Femoropopliteal — the SFA at the adductor hiatus is the commonest site; calf claudication.
Infrapopliteal (crural) — tibial/peroneal disease, typical of diabetes; threatens the foot.
3Clinical spectrum and ABPI
Symptoms progress from intermittent claudication (reproducible cramping on walking, relieved by rest) to critical limb ischaemia (rest pain worse lying flat/at night, ulceration, gangrene). Quantify severity at the bedside with the ankle-brachial pressure index (ABPI).
ABPI <0.9 — diagnostic of PAD; <0.4 suggests critical ischaemia.
ABPI >1.2 — falsely elevated by incompressible calcified vessels (diabetes, chronic kidney disease); an unreliably "normal" number in exactly the patients most at risk.
MRA is then requested to map disease before intervention.
4Aortic disease on MRA
🫀Abdominal aortic aneurysm
MRA sizes the sac and its relation to the renal arteries, but ultrasound screens (men aged 65) and CT is the standard for surgical/EVAR planning.
🩸Aortic dissection
Shows the intimal flap separating true and false lumens; but ACUTE dissection is imaged by CT angiography (faster, more available).
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRA image: axial contrast-enhanced aorta showing an intimal flap dividing a true and false lumen in a chronic descending aortic dissection.
5Why choose MRA — and its limits
Advantages: no ionising radiation and no iodinated contrast — attractive in younger patients, in iodine/contrast allergy, and for repeated follow-up. Cautions: gadolinium is linked to nephrogenic systemic fibrosis (NSF) in severe renal impairment (eGFR <30) — check renal function and use newer macrocyclic agents or avoid. MRA tends to overestimate stenosis, struggles with calcified/stented segments (stent artefact), takes longer than CT, and is contraindicated by non-MR-safe implants. Standard MRI safety applies: screen for pacemakers/ICDs, ferromagnetic implants, cochlear implants and metallic foreign bodies before scanning.
🚩 Acute limb ischaemia is a surgical emergency — the 6 Ps: Pain, Pallor, Pulselessness, Perishingly cold, Paraesthesia, Paralysis. Give IV heparin and arrange urgent revascularisation; do NOT delay for MRA. Likewise, acute aortic dissection and ruptured AAA are emergencies imaged by CT, not MRA.
🎓 Think of MRA run-off as a radiation-free road map for the leg's arterial highway: it tells the vascular team WHERE the blockage is and HOW LONG it is, which decides between a balloon (short focal lesion) and a bypass (long occlusion). But a road map is for planning a journey, not for a crash — when the limb is acutely ischaemic or the aorta is dissecting/rupturing, you act on clinical signs and CT, not MRA.
MRI__Whole Body / Functional:
Whole-body MRI (WB-MRI) sweeps the entire skeleton and its bone marrow in a single radiation-free examination. By combining T1, STIR and whole-body diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI), it exposes marrow-replacing disease long before bone is destroyed — which is why it has become the frontline whole-body scan for suspected multiple myeloma and a powerful tool for screening bony metastases.
1What the sequences show
Normal adult marrow is fatty, so it is bright on T1. When tumour cells replace that fat, the marrow becomes dark on T1 and bright on STIR and high-b DWI (a fat-suppressed, water-sensitive combination). This T1-dark / STIR-and-DWI-bright signature is the core read for both myeloma deposits and marrow metastases, and it appears while the overlying cortical bone still looks normal.
Marrow dark on T1 + bright on STIR/DWI→tumour has replaced fatty marrow
📷 Image placeholder — coronal whole-body T1 showing patchy dark focal marrow lesions in the spine and pelvis against otherwise bright fatty marrow.
2Flagship role: multiple myeloma
WB-MRI (or whole-body DWI) is now NICE-recommended first-line whole-body imaging for suspected myeloma, replacing the old plain-film skeletal survey because it is far more sensitive for marrow disease. It picks up focal marrow lesions and diffuse infiltration before any lytic destruction is visible on X-ray, and it helps distinguish smouldering from active myeloma — the presence of ≥1 unequivocal focal lesion on MRI is a myeloma-defining event that mandates treatment.
3Metastasis screening and staging
The same marrow sensitivity makes WB-MRI excellent for bone metastasis screening — classically prostate and breast deposits — and for staging lymphoma. Because there is no ionising radiation, it is well suited to young patients and to repeated monitoring of treatment response, where cumulative CT/bone-scan dose would be a concern.
4How it compares to CT and bone scan
Each modality answers a different question. CT shows lytic lesions and assesses fracture risk. A radionuclide bone scan detects osteoblastic (bone-forming) activity — so it lights up sclerotic prostate mets but is falsely negative in myeloma, which is a purely lytic/osteoclastic process with little reactive bone formation. That myeloma bone-scan trap is a favourite exam point. WB-MRI outclasses both for marrow sensitivity and whole-body coverage.
T1: tumour = dark against bright fatty marrow
STIR / high-b DWI: tumour = bright
≥1 focal MRI lesion: active (not smouldering) myeloma
🧲WB-MRI
Marrow disease — most sensitive, no radiation, whole-body. First-line for myeloma.
🩻CT
Lytic lesions and fracture risk — bony detail, but uses radiation.
☢️Bone scan
Osteoblastic activity — good for sclerotic mets, falsely negative in lytic myeloma.
📷 Image placeholder — whole-body DWI (inverted greyscale) maximum-intensity projection with multiple high-signal marrow deposits throughout the axial skeleton.
🚩
Myeloma complications are emergencies — remember CRAB: hyperCalcaemia, Renal failure, Anaemia, Bone disease. Vertebral deposits can cause spinal cord compression (back pain, leg weakness, bladder/bowel or sensory level) — this needs urgent whole-spine MRI and dexamethasone, plus consideration of pathological fracture risk. Screen every MRI patient for contraindications (pacemaker, cochlear implant, certain metallic foreign bodies/aneurysm clips) before scanning.
🎓 Exam pearl. A myeloma patient with widespread lytic disease can have a normal bone scan — myeloma is purely osteoclastic, so there is no osteoblastic tracer uptake. Use WB-MRI (or CT), never a bone scan, to assess myeloma bone disease.
Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) is a functional MRI sequence that maps the random Brownian motion of water molecules within tissue. Where water can move freely, DWI signal is low; where its motion is restricted, DWI signal is high (bright). Its power is that it turns a physiological change into a visible signal before structural change appears — most famously flagging an acute infarct within minutes, when CT is still normal. It needs no contrast and no ionising radiation.
1The DWI/ADC pair — read them together
DWI is never interpreted alone. Every DWI is paired with an ADC map (apparent diffusion coefficient), a quantitative image of how fast water is actually moving. True restriction is a lesion that is bright on DWI and dark (low) on ADC — the two must agree. Restriction happens when water is trapped: cells swell (cytotoxic oedema), tissue becomes densely packed with cells, or fluid becomes viscous. The mnemonic that anchors everything: bright DWI + dark ADC = real restriction.
Bright DWI + dark ADC→true restricted diffusion (infarct, pus, hypercellular tumour)
DWI high signal = candidate for restriction
ADC low/dark = confirms it is real
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image: paired axial DWI (b1000) and ADC map of an acute MCA infarct — the lesion is bright on DWI and correspondingly dark on ADC, confirming true restriction.
2Acute ischaemic stroke — the flagship use
In acute infarction, failure of the Na+/K+ pump drives water from the extracellular space into swelling cells — cytotoxic oedema — which restricts diffusion. DWI is the earliest and most sensitive sign of ischaemic stroke, positive within minutes and hours before CT shows anything and before T2/FLAIR change. The infarct is bright on DWI, dark on ADC. ADC pseudonormalises over the following days and eventually rises, which helps date a stroke: dark ADC means an acute/early lesion.
Sudden focal deficit, CT normal→DWI-bright / ADC-dark territory = acute infarct
3The T2 “shine-through” pitfall
DWI is built on a T2-weighted image, so a strongly T2-bright lesion (old infarct, vasogenic oedema, cyst) can look bright on DWI without any true restriction — an artefact called T2 shine-through. The trap is calling this an acute infarct. The ADC map is the arbiter: true restriction is dark on ADC; shine-through is bright/normal on ADC because water is actually moving freely. Always confirm bright DWI against the ADC before committing.
Bright DWI + bright/normal ADC→T2 shine-through, NOT restriction
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image: T2 shine-through — a chronic lesion bright on both T2/FLAIR and DWI, but with a bright (high) ADC signal, proving there is no true restriction.
4Causes of restricted diffusion
Beyond stroke, anything that packs water in tightly or fills a space with dense cells or viscous fluid restricts. The most examined discriminator is abscess vs necrotic tumour: the pus in an abscess cavity is viscous and cellular so it restricts (bright DWI, dark ADC centre), whereas the necrotic core of a tumour does not.
🧠Acute infarct
Cytotoxic oedema — earliest, most sensitive stroke sign
🦠Abscess
Viscous pus restricts — key clue vs necrotic tumour
🔬Hypercellular tumour
Lymphoma, high-grade glioma — dense cells restrict
🧩Epidermoid
Restricts — distinguishes it from an arachnoid cyst
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image: a ring-enhancing lesion whose central cavity shows bright DWI with dark ADC (restricting pus = abscess), contrasted with a necrotic tumour whose centre does not restrict.
5Oncological & whole-body DWI
Because malignant tumours are typically hypercellular, DWI is increasingly used in oncology to detect lesions (metastases, myeloma and marrow disease on whole-body DWI), to help characterise benign vs malignant tissue, and to assess treatment response — a responding tumour loses cellularity so its diffusion becomes less restricted (ADC rises). All of this without contrast, which is valuable in renal impairment.
Detect mets, lymphoma, myeloma (whole-body DWI)
Monitor response — rising ADC = falling cellularity
🚩
Two safety-critical points. Clinical: a DWI-positive / ADC-dark lesion in a patient with sudden neurological deficit is an acute infarct — activate the stroke pathway (thrombolysis/thrombectomy assessment) without waiting for CT to change; and never mistake a ring lesion with a restricting centre (abscess) for a tumour. MRI safety: the magnet is always on — screen every patient for pacemakers/ICDs, cochlear implants, aneurysm clips and intra-orbital metallic foreign bodies; loose ferromagnetic objects become lethal projectiles.
🎓The single highest-yield rule: bright DWI is only meaningful once the ADC confirms it. Dark ADC = true restriction (acute infarct, abscess, hypercellular tumour); bright/normal ADC = T2 shine-through, an impostor. Get into the habit of reading the pair together every time.

Functional MRI (fMRI) maps brain activity, not just structure. It exploits the BOLD (Blood-Oxygen-Level-Dependent) signal to show which regions of cortex "light up" when a person performs a task or simply rests, and its headline clinical role is pre-surgical planning — locating eloquent cortex so a surgeon can remove a lesion without leaving a patient with a new deficit.

1The BOLD principle — why active brain lights up

When neurons fire, local metabolic demand rises and the brain over-compensates by increasing regional blood flow, delivering a surplus of oxyhaemoglobin. The MRI signal changes because oxy- and deoxy-haemoglobin have different magnetic properties:

Neuronal activity & more oxygenated blood→less paramagnetic deoxyhaemoglobin locally → brighter T2*-weighted signal → that voxel appears activated
Oxyhaemoglobin = diamagnetic — barely distorts the local field.
Deoxyhaemoglobin = paramagnetic — distorts the field and reduces signal; as it washes out, signal rises.
The BOLD signal is therefore an indirect, haemodynamic proxy for neuronal firing, not a direct electrical recording.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the fMRI image: axial brain slice with a coloured statistical activation "blob" overlaid on greyscale structural MRI during a finger-tapping task, showing contralateral primary motor cortex lighting up.
2Task-based vs resting-state acquisition

Two broad ways to run the scan, both looking at the same BOLD signal:

🎯Task-based fMRI
Patient performs a task in the scanner (e.g. finger tapping for motor cortex, word/verb generation or naming for language). Activation during task is contrasted against rest.
🧩Resting-state fMRI
No task — spontaneous low-frequency BOLD fluctuations reveal functional connectivity and intrinsic networks (e.g. the default mode network). Useful when a patient cannot cooperate.
3Clinical & research uses
Pre-surgical planning (main clinical use): map eloquent cortex — motor, sensory and language areas (e.g. Broca's and Wernicke's) — adjacent to a brain tumour or epileptogenic focus, so resection spares them and avoids post-operative deficits.
Lateralising language and memory: a non-invasive alternative or adjunct to the Wada test (intracarotid amobarbital) for determining the dominant hemisphere.
Research: cognition, and resting-state functional connectivity / brain networks.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the fMRI image: pre-surgical language-mapping fMRI during a verb-generation task showing left-lateralised Broca's area activation sitting immediately anterior to a frontal glioma, used to plan the resection margin.
4Limitations & MRI safety
Indirect measure — reflects haemodynamics, not neuronal firing directly.
Lower temporal resolution — the BOLD response lags neural activity by seconds.
Highly motion-sensitive and needs a cooperative patient for task paradigms.
Specialised, not routine — used in selected neurosurgical and research settings.
MRI safety applies: strong static magnetic field means screening for ferromagnetic implants, pacemakers/ICDs (unless MR-conditional), cochlear implants, aneurysm clips and metallic foreign bodies; no free metal in the room; hearing protection for gradient noise.
🚩 fMRI is a functional adjunct for surgical planning: the whole point is to avoid a post-operative neurological deficit by identifying eloquent cortex adjacent to a lesion before the surgeon operates. It does not replace clinical judgement or intra-operative mapping.
🎓 Remember the physics in one line: active neurons → more oxyhaemoglobin (diamagnetic) → less paramagnetic deoxyhaemoglobin → brighter BOLD signal. Structural MRI shows you where the tumour is; fMRI shows you what the brain next to it does.

Fetal MRI is a second-line, problem-solving test. Antenatal ultrasound is always first-line; when US detects an abnormality that needs further characterisation — most often of the fetal brain/CNS — MRI is used to refine the diagnosis, sharpen the prognosis and inform counselling and delivery/surgical planning through the fetal-medicine MDT.

1Where it sits: after ultrasound, not instead of it

US is cheap, real-time, widely available and the screening/diagnostic workhorse of pregnancy. MRI is reserved for cases where US is equivocal or incomplete — poor acoustic windows (maternal obesity, oligohydramnios), late-gestation ossified fetal skull limiting brain views, or a lesion whose full extent changes management. It adds tissue characterisation and a large field of view that US cannot always achieve.

US shows isolated ventriculomegaly→MRI to look for associated agenesis of the corpus callosum, migrational or posterior fossa anomalies
2Why it is safe: no ionising radiation, no gadolinium

MRI uses no ionising radiation and is considered safe in pregnancy, usually performed in the 2nd or 3rd trimester when the fetus is large enough to image well. Gadolinium contrast is avoided — it crosses the placenta, is excreted into amniotic fluid, recirculates and is associated with adverse outcomes; fetal MRI is therefore a non-contrast study.

Fast sequences — single-shot fast spin-echo T2 acquires each slice in a fraction of a second, effectively "freezing" fetal motion without needing sedation.
Natural contrast — bright amniotic fluid outlines the fetus; T2 gives excellent grey/white matter and CSF contrast for the CNS.

3Key indications, region by region

The dominant use is the CNS, but MRI also problem-solves chest, neck, abdomen and placenta.

🧠CNS (commonest)
Ventriculomegaly, agenesis of the corpus callosum, posterior fossa anomalies (Dandy-Walker), cortical malformations.
🩻Spine
Neural tube defects / spina bifida with Chiari II; MRI helps plan fetal or postnatal surgery.
🫁Chest
Congenital diaphragmatic hernia — measure lung volumes for prognosis; CPAM characterisation.
👶Neck
Airway-threatening masses (teratoma, lymphatic malformation) — plan an EXIT procedure.
🩸Placenta
Placenta accreta spectrum — assess depth of invasion and haemorrhage risk before delivery.
👯Twins
Complications of monochorionic twins (e.g. brain injury after TTTS or co-twin demise).

4What it changes: counselling and planning

MRI rarely stands alone — it feeds the fetal-medicine MDT. By refining diagnosis and prognosis it informs parental counselling (including decisions about termination of pregnancy), the choice between fetal versus postnatal surgery, and where and how to deliver (e.g. a tertiary centre with neonatal surgery, or an EXIT-to-airway delivery).

🚩 Findings that change delivery planning demand specialist fetal-medicine/MDT management: an airway-threatening neck mass (needs an EXIT procedure to secure the airway on placental circulation), severe congenital diaphragmatic hernia, or high-risk placenta accreta spectrum (potential for massive obstetric haemorrhage requiring a planned caesarean with surgical and blood-bank support).
🎓 Remember the hierarchy: ultrasound first, MRI to problem-solve — most often the fetal brain. It is safe (no ionising radiation), performed 2nd/3rd trimester, and never uses gadolinium because it crosses the placenta. Its value is not just a prettier picture but better prognostication, counselling and delivery/surgical planning.

Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) is an advanced MRI diffusion technique that measures the directionality (anisotropy) of water diffusion. In white-matter tracts, water diffuses preferentially along the axon bundles (anisotropic diffusion) rather than equally in all directions. DTI captures this direction and magnitude and uses it to reconstruct 3D white-matter tracts — a process called tractography — usually displayed as colour-coded fibre maps. Its headline clinical role is neurosurgical planning: showing the surgeon where eloquent tracts run so they can be preserved during tumour resection.

1
The Physical Principle

In free fluid (e.g. CSF), water diffuses equally in every direction — isotropic diffusion. Inside an organised white-matter tract, axonal membranes and myelin constrain movement, so water moves fastest along the fibre and is restricted across it — anisotropic diffusion. DTI models this directional behaviour at each voxel as a tensor (an ellipsoid), whose long axis points along the dominant fibre direction.

Diffusion equal in all directions
→
Isotropic — low anisotropy (CSF, grey matter)
Diffusion channelled along fibres
→
Anisotropic — high anisotropy (organised white-matter tracts)
2
Reading the Colour Map

Tractography reconstructs and colour-codes fibres by their principal direction of diffusion. Learn the standard convention — it is a common exam sticking point:

↔️
Red
Left–right (transverse). Classic example: the corpus callosum.
↕️
Green
Anterior–posterior. Example: association fibres running front–back.
⬆️
Blue
Superior–inferior (cranio-caudal). Example: the corticospinal tracts.
3
Fractional Anisotropy (FA)

Fractional anisotropy (FA) is a scalar (0–1) that quantifies how directional the diffusion is at each voxel — in practice a marker of tract integrity.

High FA (near 1)
→
Highly organised, intact, well-myelinated tracts
Reduced FA
→
Loss of organisation — tract disruption, damage or demyelination
Reduced FA is sensitive but non-specific: it tells you a tract is damaged, not the cause. Axonal loss, demyelination, oedema and infiltration by tumour can all lower FA.

4
Clinical Uses
🧠
Neurosurgical planning
The main clinical use. Maps major tracts — corticospinal tract, arcuate fasciculus (language), optic radiations — around a tumour so they can be preserved and post-operative deficits avoided. Complements fMRI, which maps grey-matter function, while DTI maps the white-matter wiring connecting it.
🔬
White-matter integrity
Assessing diffuse damage: diffuse axonal injury in traumatic brain injury, demyelination in multiple sclerosis, and research into neurodegeneration via tract-based studies.
5
Limitations
Crossing fibres in one voxel
→
Simple tensor model can misrepresent them — a key weakness
Indirect, model-based
→
Reconstructed tracts are inferences, not literal images of axons
Specialised / research-heavy
→
Needs dedicated acquisition and post-processing; not a routine sequence
🚩
The value is surgical — preserve eloquent tracts. DTI earns its place by keeping the neurosurgeon off the pathways that cause deficits: injure the corticospinal tract and you cause a motor deficit / weakness; injure the arcuate fasciculus and you cause a language deficit; injure the optic radiations and you cause a visual field defect. And because it is an MRI technique, standard MRI safety applies — strong static magnet at all times, ferromagnetic/implant screening, and no unsafe pacemakers, cochlear implants or metallic foreign bodies.
🎓 Pearl: Remember the colour code with “RGB = the three axes”: Red left–right, Green anterior–posterior, Blue superior–inferior. Then pair each surgical tract with the deficit it protects against — corticospinal (blue, motor), arcuate (language), optic radiations (vision) — and you have both the physics and the clinical punchline in one breath.
